items.body:
A quiet show of strength from Chicago’s budding and already highly sought after Dub Techno specialists, Kino Disk, hustling 11 exclusive permutations of dub-suffixed ambient, techno, and elemental abstraction by label regulars and new figures including Eustress, Infant, 8004 and many others, huge tip FFO Chain Reaction, Huerco S., Echospace, Short Span, Vialan.

In the space of 20 odd releases since 2024, Kino Disk has emerged as a key point of interest for off-grid dub aficionados. ‘American Dub Electronics’ now opens an ideal entry portal to their microcosm, rendering 11 exclusive bits that speak to the label’s fine grasp of variation within a theme. Trust it’s not wall-to-wall mark & moritz worship, rather a webbed spectra of interrelated, American POV’s on the same gauzy spirit from their collected vapours.

Building on the smouldering embers of over 30 years of precedents in this field, the set sways from the moonlit tidal movement of Psalm Star Electric’s ‘001’ to the unmoored slosh of 8006 (whose ‘8004’ was a sleeper gem of ’25) with a particularly nocturnal appeal. Eustress practices the most Catholic form of dub house in the darkly luminous ‘mm’, and Eden Aurelius’ Ring impress with the ASMR-like sensitivities of ‘Changeling’, and another label regular Point Survey with the phasing dub noise of ‘Print-Through’.

Keener observers may recognise those names already, but perhaps not the new ones here, notably Corbin Cary & Taylor White’s Permutia duo, secreting the fine lather chords and sandman bassline of ‘p1.2’, or HPIN with the early SND-style puckered glitch of ‘Remote’, Uos’ washed-out textures on Uos in ‘Uos Jelly’, and dreamily poised dub waltz of ‘Speedwalker’ by a.m.p & b.p.p.
items._cn_summary: 这是芝加哥厂牌Kino Disk推出的合辑，收录11首独家曲目，展现其对dub技术美学的多向拓展。作品并非对经典dub techno的简单模仿，而是以环境、噪声、微声和律动元素交织，构建出从月光般潮汐流动到失重晃动、从暗黑发光到底噪颗粒的丰富光谱。参与艺术家包括Eustress、Infant、8004、Point Survey等厂牌常客，也有Permutia、HPIN、Uos等新面孔，各自以不同方式处理延迟、混响与空间层次，呈现美国视角下对dub精神的松散诠释。整体听感偏夜行、沉浸，兼具身体律动与抽象聆听的双重属性，适合关注当代电子音乐实验方向的听众。

Enigmatic audity Aisie returns five years on from a strange, overlooked debut with a new suite of compressed atmospheres highly tipped FFO False Aralia, Eliza B.C., Thought Broadcast, Civilistjävel!, Hazyville-era Actress.

‘Black Fire Dream’ picks up from where 2021’s ‘Halcyon Gang Poet’ left us in a surreal, uncanny valley state of mind. The seven part, 30 minute mini-LP continues to fascinate with its cyborganic nature and dreamy otherworldliness, luring down gauzily textured, fractal wormholes where samples of “obscure educational science shows, ghost station radio transmissions, vinyl record detritus and blown-out microscopic field recordings” are gently reanimated and transmuted with a poetic sorcery. 

The whole thing feels as though it were conjuured without human touch, like the inner thoughts of an AI or machines autonomously air-syncing and executing their functions in private. With incremental stealth it breezes by in a hypnagogic haze, half-heard melodies sprouting and dissolving into the aether as granular rhythms buckle and trickle. Eyes will likely be at half mast by the end of the A-side, all the best to receive the B-side’s suggestive, illusive shadowplay of smoke and mirrors refraction and a final slope off into something like a chopped and screwed echo of Topdown Dialectic.
items._cn_summary: Aisie时隔五年带来续作，将碎片化采样——包括冷门科教节目片段、幽灵电台信号、黑胶唱片残片与失真的微观田野录音——以诗意的方式重新激活，编织出具有机器意识般的超现实音景。七首曲目、约三十分钟的篇幅在催眠般的迷雾中展开，半成型的旋律萌芽又消散，颗粒化节奏起伏不定，营造出一种仿佛AI内心独白的非人类触感。专辑延续了前作的超现实氛围，但更加成熟，B面以烟雾与镜面般的折射手法收束，最终滑入类似Topdown Dialectic的切碎减速回声。对于偏好声景探索、模糊噪音与暗潮边缘质感的听众而言，这是一张值得细听的文本密集型作品。

items.body:
Coltrane’s invigorating ’66 spiritual free jazz salvo - the follow-up to ‘A Love Supreme’ (1965) - is unleashed from the Verve Vault, spotlighting his classic line-up tearing out on templates set by Ornette Coleman years prior, along with more reserved moments of beauty. An evergreen..

"Following the genre-redefining revelations of A Love Supreme in 1965, John Coltrane began a dramatic shift toward spiritual free jazz, abandoning familiar forms in favour of a more abstract sonic palette and bold questions he'd spend the rest of his life and career pursuing. Meditations, released by Impulse! in 1966, continues that emotional throughline while retaining, for the last time in full, the classic quartet that propelled Trane to greatness: pianist McCoy Tyner, bassist Jimmy Garrison and drummer Elvin Jones. (They're further augmented by Pharoah Sanders on tenor sax and additional drummer Rashied Ali.) Meditations pushes Coltrane’s spiritual jazz into heightened realms of energy and abstraction — a powerful document of transformation, intensity, and devotion in Coltrane’s recorded legacy."
items._cn_summary: 这张1966年的专辑是Coltrane继《A Love Supreme》之后向精神自由爵士全面转向的重要记录，延续了Ornette Coleman开创的无调性即兴路径。经典四重奏阵容——钢琴McCoy Tyner、贝斯Jimmy Garrison、鼓Elvin Jones——最后一次以完整编制出现在录音中，并加入了次中音萨克斯手Pharoah Sanders与第二鼓手Rashied Ali。专辑在高能抽象段落与静谧沉思段落之间交替，将自由爵士推向更极端的能量密度与精神探索维度。两位鼓手的双鼓配置制造出层次丰富的节奏张力，五重奏的集体即兴充满爆发力与仪式感。整张作品是Coltrane艺术生涯中转型期的关键文献，兼具原始力量与冥想式的内在深度。

items.body: Across eight untitled pieces, fold/interval develops a musical language in which guitar dyads, granular electronics, filtered resonances and microscopic digital artefacts coexist within carefully articulated sonic environments. By directing attention towards the behaviour of sound itself, its texture, spectral balance and the constantly shifting relationships between one resonance and the next, Giuseppe Ielasi and Fabio Perletta engage in an open exchange that is equally balanced and coherent. The title of the project itself offers an illuminating point of entry. In audio synthesis, wavefolding is a process in which a signal exceeding a certain threshold is folded back onto itself, generating new harmonics and increasingly complex timbral structures instead of simply clipping or distorting. The second half of the title is equally revealing. Throughout the album, Giuseppe Ielasi’s guitar is reduced to two-note dyads—musical intervals—whose quiet interjections provide the elementary material from which Fabio Perletta’s electronic processes unfold. Fold describes a continuous process of sonic transformation; interval refers both to the guitar’s harmonic vocabulary and to the spaces separating successive sonic events. The music continually inhabits both meanings. The dialogue between Ielasi and Perletta never feels predetermined. Repeated figures evolve through minute changes in density, frequency and perspective, while silence functions as an active compositional force, shaping every gesture with remarkable precision. Listening gradually shifts away from isolated sonic events towards intervals in both senses of the word: the relationships between pitches and the spaces separating sounds. Tiny overtone fluctuations, delicate feedback and almost imperceptible transients continually redefine the surrounding acoustic field. Giulia Bruno‘s photographic contribution is integral to the project. Her images of landscapes, architectural structures and technological infrastructures mirror the music’s fascination with hidden systems, suspended attention and processes unfolding beneath the threshold of immediate perception. Sound and image share the same temporal logic, encouraging prolonged observation rather than instant recognition. Ultimately, fold/interval is a record about relationships: between acoustic and electronic sound, presence and absence, transformation and stasis. Every gesture appears with an acute sense of proportion. Like the wavefolding process evoked in its title, it reveals how complexity can emerge from the continuous reshaping of the simplest materials. giulia bruno (self portrait giulia bruno) To find out more we have spoken directly with Ielasi, Perletta and Bruno. Untitled (1–8) feels poised between presence and absence: Giuseppe’s sparse guitar gestures seem to emerge from and dissolve back into Fabio’s electronic textures, while Giulia’s photographs introduce a parallel visual rhythm. How did the three of you develop a shared language across sound and image, and at what point did the project become more than a musical collaboration and evolve into fold/interval itself? Giulia Bruno: fold/interval was born from the desire to create together within a free and anti-hierarchical relational context, where sounds and images can also follow a shared path, without subordination. Our relationship began with mutual respect and with a friendship that developed over time. Recognizing ourselves in what each of us does — and perhaps also in who each of us is through our work — created a solid foundation from which the desire emerged to explore something unexpected together, grounded in a shared trust in looking and listening. The project therefore arises from the desire to bring together thoughts, sensibilities, and intuitions that find their form through shared sounds, images, and silences. Fabio Perletta: fold/interval was never just a musical project; rather, it started as a trio. Before that, Giuseppe and I had been discussing the possibility of collaborating in a broader sense. Giulia and Giuseppe already knew each other well, having collaborated for a long time, so everything naturally found its way into fold/interval, which was conceived as a space for exchange involving different practices and sensibilities, where sound and image could develop together. We aim to find a shared space where listening and looking can influence each other, and where unexpected connections could emerge. The music and the photographs are not separate layers, but different manifestations of a shared process and vision. Giuseppe Ielasi: I have been working with Giulia, on different projects, for more than 15 years. This was mainly on film or installation works. More recently we started discussing about possible live performances, and our first one as a duo happened in June 2025 at the Triennale in Milano. We loved it, but at the same time felt the need to work on something less structured, more open to improvisation and surprises. I also know Fabio since a long time: we shared a few concerts and he published some of my music on 901editions, but most of all we exchanged thoughts, music and spent a lot of time together in the last years. We were ready for a collaboration and started playing and recording together. It was very natural, then, to merge those projects, introducing Giulia to Fabio. My impression is that the shared language was already there, it was just a matter of making things happen. fabio perletta (photo oyamada kuniya) The release includes photographs ranging from natural and architectural environments to technological infrastructures, including an image of the cooling systems of the Barcelona Supercomputing Center. Given the increasing debate around the environmental cost of AI and large-scale computation, were these infrastructures approached primarily as visual forms, or do they also function as reflections on the invisible systems that increasingly shape contemporary life and knowledge production? GB: My work never approaches images solely as visual forms. Rather, the image is a pretext for activation: a way of bringing to light contemporary questions concerning collective issues, research processes, and systems of relation. In this sense, I am interested in deconstructing the aesthetics of the image, removing it from spectacle so that it can become an activator. An activator of processes of change and reflection on how we observe, recognize, and respond to different forms of violence and contradiction. I believe we are often suspended within a constant tension: between hypnosis and impotence, between beauty and fear, between systems of seduction and power and critical awareness. This is why I am interested in working with the landscape — whether natural, technological, architectural, infrastructural, human, or relational — as a space to be read, questioned, and traversed. The infrastructures, and what is reactivated through photography, are therefore not merely formal presences, but signals of broader, often invisible systems that condition the way we live, know, and imagine the future, within an obsessive system of continuous archiving. To look also means asking ourselves what choices we can make in order to build a collectivity capable of coexisting, resisting, and generating new forms of relation. FP: I believe this connection is at the core of fold/interval. The project does not come from a desire to blindly produce new images and sounds, but rather to create a space where attention can be reactivated and where different, heightened forms of perception coexist. We are not interested in spectacularization, our focus is on cultivating attention. The way we work together is based on a process of listening and waiting, allowing each element to emerge without forcing relationships or creating predetermined correspondences. We were drawn to what happens in the space between things: between the visible and the hidden, between what is heard and what is left in silence. In this sense, fold/interval reflects a resistance to the acceleration and saturation that define contemporary production and consumption. This first work seeks to open up a different temporal dimension—one where the viewer and listener are invited to sit with uncertainty, observe the details, and forge their own connections. giuseppe ielasi (photo philip ielasi) The music is remarkably restrained. Guitar notes and chords seem to drift through digital circuitry, leaving large amounts of space between events. Was reduction a conscious compositional strategy from the outset, or did the pieces gradually arrive at this sparse form through a process of subtraction and editing? FP: From my perspective, it is a combination of both. The way Giuseppe and I approach sound within this project stems from a shared interest in creating an environment where every element holds its own weight and presence, allowing unexpected encounters to unfold. Reduction wasn’t a conscious aesthetic choice; it emerged from a desire to let the space breathe and become an active component of the composition. Silence, resonance, and the intervals between events are not mere voids, but structural pillars that give sounds the room to reveal their intrinsic qualities. At the same time, this sparseness was already baked into the sounds we each brought to the table. Giuseppe’s guitar—with its precision and abstract quality—and my stylized electronic textures, which are often pushed toward the extreme areas of the spectrum, come from very different yet complimentary worlds. Throughout the process, we constantly sought an organic balance between these two worlds, letting the clarity and subtle details of the guitar interact with the ambiguity and roughness of the electronics. GI: It’s strange, the music doesn’t feel that restrained to me. There’s constant activity in it, lots of repetitions (but no loops) and the pacing and placing are very deliberate, but somehow the flow feels very natural (the idea of ‘restrain’ somehow suggest that it was ‘forced’, and that is not the case). There was little subtraction, and almost no editing. We suggested basic materials and layers and realized that many of those could co-exist and interacts very naturally. It was a very intuitive, non-formalised process. Giulia, many of your recent texts engage with questions of technological mediation, the overproduction of images, and the difficulty of maintaining spaces of reflection within contemporary systems of visibility. Do you see a connection between those concerns and the aesthetic choices behind Untitled (1–8), which often feels like it is resisting speed, saturation and information overload in favour of slowness, ambiguity and attention? GB: We are connected by a shared way of thinking: the desire not to follow the logics of production, seduction, and spectacularization, but rather the rhythm of our own thought and listening. It is a natural gaze, made of layers but not oversaturation, of words expressed with care, and of a constant search for coherence. There are no predetermined rules or rigid orders of thought, but rather a natural transformation that emerges from the attempt to remove the work from what is immediately displayed. We are interested in what remains suspended, what requires time, what does not immediately offer itself only as an image or as information. The reflection on the macrosystems in which we move as individuals runs through our thinking and our gaze, and also shapes the way we relate to others. Untitled (1–8) emerges from this attention: from the desire to create a space in which sound, image, and word can slow down perception and open up the possibility of a shared rereading of the processes that involve us. FP: I am drawn to the word Giulia mentioned: rhythm. Our biological rhythm—the intrinsic time we need to process our surroundings—differs for everyone, but it is undeniably a means of survival in this violent, vulgar world. To honor it requires welcoming the complex, the unexpected, the unheard, and the unseen. We aim to stay close to this idea, not in a literal, romantic, or strictly political sense, but as a practice that resists the pressure to produce immediate meaning or visibility. Giulia’s reflection on overproduction and the saturation of images deeply informs how we approach both sound and vision: not as materials to be quickly consumed, but as processes demanding time. The project seeks to create a space where perception can remain open and non-finalised, where things are not immediately resolved into information or representation. Instead, it sustains an alternative internal tempo—one that allows for hesitation, repetition, and return. fold/interval is described not only as an audiovisual project but also as a publishing platform. Beyond this first release, how do you envision the project developing? Are future editions likely to continue exploring the relationship between image, sound and material publication, or do you see fold/interval evolving into a broader framework for collaborations, research projects and new commissions? GB: Starting from the coming together of our conversations, we did not want to place any limit on the project’s transformation. We believe in a path made of coherence, but also of responses to research processes that can change, expand, and take on new forms over time, just as we ourselves change over time. For us, collaboration means first and foremost engaging in dialogue and confrontation. We have not placed any limit on this exchange, except for the desire to do it with people who share with us a vision of the world in which aesthetics is never placed above relationships, research, and the search for meaning in life. In this sense, fold/interval may continue to explore the relationship between image, sound, and material publication, but it may also open itself to other forms: collaborations, research, commissions, dialogues, and processes that have not yet been anticipated. What interests us is that it remains a living space, capable of transforming without losing coherence. FP: For me, fold/interval is less of a fixed container and more of an open ecology, inherently built to evolve. The idea of the publishing platform naturally stems from a desire to give a physical, tangible form to time and thought, which is why the material aspect will always remain a core interest. Looking ahead, I imagine fold/interval evolving as a flexible framework that could manifest as a physical edition, a sound installation, a research residency, or simply a space for shared dialogue. Future editions might not always look or sound the same, it will simply follow the needs of the encounters and questions that emerge along the way. GI: What interests me is to collaborate on a project that’s very open, hard to define and might even be confusing at times. We released an edition with a cd and a set of photos, a short film on our website and we’re co-curating some events and sound installations at “settantaventidue” in Milano. But we also exist as a label / publishing platform (more editions, with or without music, might appear soon and those could include other collaborators) and we’re planning some concerts, residencies and installations for the next months. So, yes, it’s definitely evolving and I’m very curious to see what will happen. (Gianmarco Del Re)
items._cn_summary: fold/interval 在八首无标题作品中构建了一套精密的声音语法：吉他的双音音程作为最小素材，经颗粒电子、滤波共振与微观数字痕迹处理后展开。Ielasi 的稀疏拨弦在 Perletta 的电子纹理中浮现又消融，沉默被用作主动的作曲力量，反复出现的动机通过密度、频率与视角的细微变化缓慢演化。评论将标题拆解为'折叠'与'间隔'双义——前者指波形的连续变形，后者同时涵盖和声语言与声响事件之间的留白空间。Giulia Bruno 的摄影以建筑、技术基础设施与景观影像呼应音乐的隐藏系统美学。整张专辑关注关系本身：声学与电子、在场与缺席、转化与静止，复杂性源自最简材料的持续重塑。

items.body: All in all, a very good introduction to Eighth Tower’s substantial catalog for lovers of deep electronic sound art. Quite recommended while reading Margaret Murray’s acclaimed history of European witchcraft. Related to the occult, divine arts, magic, and the supernatural Witchcraft & Black Magic In The United Kingdom (Expanded Version) by Various Artists   Over the years, the Italian indie label Eighth Tower Records has covered an important amount of themes related to the occult, divine arts, magic, and the supernatural, from historical facts to popular culture (cinema, literature). These topics serve as the conceptual background of many collective releases that feature a number of sound artists from the same family circle (most of them have also published individual releases separately for the label). Titled Witchcraft & Black Magic in United Kingdom, this release is part of the whole concept, but focuses here on witch hunts during the severe repressive years of the Inquisition practiced in a Puritan Anglican Great Britain, notably during the English Civil War. We can remember famous cases during the late medieval and early Renaissance periods, under the cruel activities of Matthew Hopkins toward those accused of renewing a pact with the devil. There is a vast iconography linked to this dark era (Baldung…) and it has also been put on screen a hundred times, as in Witchfinder General, Cry of the Banshee, and Blood on Satan’s Claw. Haunting aural and sonic explorations :: The album is delivered as an extended version of a previous edition released back in 2019. For listeners who are not familiar with this label, it is owned by Raffaele Pezzella (alias Sonologyst), and it has gained a solid reputation over the years thanks to numerous collaborations, reissues… which enrich the field of subterranean dark ambient music and post-industrial sound experimentalism. This version of the album welcomes exclusive tracks by Dead Voices On Air, Mario Lino Stancati and 400 Lonely Things. The musical production embraces haunting aural and sonic explorations, with experimentation on timbres, tone colors, acoustic instrumentation and processed concrete noises. A piece such as “The Village” by the legendary Rapoon is really emblematic of the album, for its soundtrack-like tendency, foggy, echoing acoustic strings and ominous proportions. A personal favorite on this album is the hauntological, ghostly and distorted “Crypt of Saint John” by Howlround. The whole thing is deeply cinematic, evocative, enthralling, abstract and cerebral, with rare moments of suspenseful melodicism. All in all, a very good introduction to Eighth Tower’s substantial catalog for lovers of deep electronic sound art. Quite recommended while reading Margaret Murray’s acclaimed history of European witchcraft. Witchcraft & Black Magic In The United Kingdom (Expanded Version) is available on Eighth Tower. Moving through modernized, mechanized electronic flutter Such sleek, rhythmic glitch sees rinse.repeat at it again with this oversized extended player, running just over twenty-four minutes and moving through modernized, mechanized electronic flutter, opening with “ERR_LOOP: Pleasant Failure.” After all this time, its “errors,” under an imprint committed to keeping them “clean,” continue to cultivate minute sonic acrobatics from start to finish. With its second volume leaning into what could be further musical constructs, “SWEET_CORRUPT” glides along through minimal technoid shifts, while the Arovane-leaning “The Last Pattern We Shared” and “AXM_02::LOOP_DESYNC” work through a relaxed infusion of bleep-breaks. The back-half triplet of Brain Axiom Vol.2 dissolves into an accumulation of everything that has come before: “A Feeling With No Output” brings tonal color, “BRAINMAP_FRAGMENT_v3” flickers through beat-driven landscapes, and closer “CRPT_SEQ:AXM” pushes it all toward a sweetly melancholic (and slightly disjointed) intersection, bringing everything together with focused restraint. system.log>>> [Recovered audio signature matches AXIOM-Vol.2-grade entropy]>>> [Loop recursion depth: INCREASING]>>> [System awareness protocol: ACTIVATED]>>> [Pattern self-recognition: CONFIRMED]ERROR SIGNATURE: [///loop:remember:feel:break]░▒▓██▒▒░┈┈┈┈──> Brain Axiom Vol.2 complete. <──┈┈┈▒██▓▒░░⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿the machine now knows it is broken.and that knowledge is the only beautiful thing left.⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿  Brain Axiom Vol.2 is available on Clean Error. items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — The inclusion of soprano Marie-Anne Pollaris added a new ingredient to the concoction brewed by Roger Trigaux's band, complementing the King Crimson-esque influences found in the electric guitar work and the atonal piano, courtesy of Alain Rochette. Ferdinand Philippot's bass lines, characterized by the fluid dynamics of jazz-rock fusión, paired seamlessly with Daniel Denis's drumming, which could just as easily support a waltz as it could navigate the most intricate, shifting passages. All of this lends Le poison qui rend fou, Pt. 1: Ram Ram va faire "Pif Paf" its avant-garde flair, evoking an almost cinematic atmosphere, like stepping onto the ledge of an abandoned building, or recalling the dark, modern waltz-like movements found in the Bob Fosse choreography of All That Jazz.When the piano stands alone, it is chamber music... but as the guitar enters while the piano continues, an imperial atmosphere emerges. One imagines that, faced with such a soundscape, the floor simply has to open up and reveal a doorway to another world, which is the concept behind The Poison That Causes Madness.The idea of a modern ballet is actually very fitting, because one can envision a choreography for Ersatz, syncopated, fragmented, broken, dismantled... assembled... and dismantled once more. The piano, the drums, the guitar, they are all disjointed parts that, together, fail to form anything concrete... and yet, within that lack of synchronization, something is found: a message, a breath of life. Another, alternative mode of expression."Le poison qui rend fou, Pt. 2: Didi, dans ta chambre!" presents something circus-like... something pathetic, an old theatrical performance where the protagonists are not up on stage but down below. The dynamic between the electric guitar and the piano is in constant flux, up, down, inducing vertigo; and that is the point: to find no rest, no calm, no refuge. That is the nature of the avant-garde, as someone once said, someone who might well have lost their sanity through such intense contact with art. It is a fire that burns, yet one cannot help but draw near, like insects to a light, while the piano plays on, creating a dense, alarming atmosphere that is decidedly not rock. Urgency is the Word, urgency to speak, to remain silent, but above all to express oneself... in one way or another.An ominous atmosphere ushers in the album's finale with "Samana"; yet, a spirited fusion bassline and atonal piano, vibrant even as the music winds down, embark on a futile quest across a disorienting landscape. Suddenly, calm takes hold, giving way to a suite, an ode to madness. It brings to mind Erasmus of Rotterdam's In Praise of Folly, where stepping outside the boundaries was seen as healthy, as well as Philippe de Broca's film Le Roi de Coeur (1966). All these works speak to the same theme, while piano and guitar trace an invisible line connecting the white of the eye directly to the red of the heart, leaving behind that essential note of unease and intrigue.

items._cn_summary: 这是一张1985年由Roger Trigaux领军的RIO/Avant-Prog专辑，乐评围绕三首长曲展开。第一部分以无调性钢琴、电吉他与爵士律动贝斯线交织，营造出近乎电影的氛围，键盘独处时呈现室内乐质地，吉他加入后转向帝国般的庄严。第二部分呈现马戏团式的病态戏剧感，钢琴与电吉他持续起伏制造眩晕，密集紧迫的织体远离摇滚传统。最终章以不安的开场引入融合贝斯线，结尾转向平静的组曲，宛若致敬疯狂本身。整张专辑以断裂、错位、解构为美学核心，将零碎片段拼合出无法被单一风格定义的表现形式。评论长度充足，文学化描述密集，但内容在文末明显被截断。

items.body: Atrición is the sort of record that seems to have been built under fluorescent light, with the smell of disinfectant somewhere nearby and history banging its head against the walls. Santiago Nicolás wrote much of it in an oncology center, and that circumstance hangs over the album with a terrible physical clarity. The body here is material: cells change, systems fail, pressure accumulates, and time works patiently on everything it touches. Nicolás places that fact beside political violence, invasion, borders, archives, and inherited trauma, finding a shared logic in processes that advance by occupation and erosion rather than spectacle. That could have produced a record swollen with significance. Instead, Atrición stays severe, compact, and rhythmically exact. Its drums hit with the blunt economy of DAF and Nitzer Ebb, while the synths carry the cold forward motion of contemporary techno. Suicide lurks in the repetition, Cabaret Voltaire in the sense that machinery can become a social instrument, and Schwefelgelb in the clipped, bodily momentum. Nicolás keeps tightening the screws until repetition stops feeling like recurrence and starts behaving like pressure. This is where the album becomes genuinely nasty in the best sense. A beat returns, a distorted percussion figure acquires another layer, a synthesizer line keeps digging into the same patch of ground, and suddenly you understand accumulation as an experience rather than a concept. Violence, in this framework, survives through systems, habits, documents, buildings, borders, and bodies that continue carrying its consequences after the visible event has passed. Atrición makes persistence feel physical. The lyrics explore themes of archives, silence, trauma, and accountability without resorting to slogans. Nicolás prefers metaphor, allowing the songs to hover between personal memory and public history. His focus is on transmission—what is passed down through generations, what institutions preserve by omission, and what a body retains despite efforts to erase it. The music responds with persistent repetition, reminiscent of bureaucracy but driven by a punchy kick drum. By the end, Atrición feels like a controlled study in pressure: biological, political, historical, rhythmic. Catastrophe often advances by degrees, through small permissions and repeated injuries. He builds music for that recognition, and the result is frightening precisely because it moves with such discipline, until pressure itself becomes its own evidence. Listen to Atrición below and order the EP here. Atrición by Santiago Nicolás Nicolás has spent more than a decade moving through electronic music, noise, experimental composition, and post-punk, including work with The Deadly Affair, Access Device, Ángel de la Guarda, and Föllakzoid’s live lineup. Atrición compresses that experience into a language of hard surfaces and accumulating force. The production is clean enough to expose every impact, yet abrasive enough to keep the record from becoming sterile. Follow Santiago Nicolás: Bandcamp Instagram The post Chilean Techno-Industrial Producer Santiago Nicolás Performs an Autopsy on Trauma in “Atrición” EP appeared first on Post-Punk.com.
items._cn_summary: 智利制作人Santiago Nicolás在肿瘤中心完成了这张EP，将身体的损耗与政治暴力、边境、档案等议题并置，以共同的逻辑呈现它们如何通过侵占与侵蚀推进。音乐上采用紧凑而精确的节奏型态，鼓击延续了DAF与Nitzer Ebb式的冷硬经济，合成器则带有当代techno的前推力。重复被作为压力手段而非简单循环使用，每一层失真打击或合成器线条的叠加都在制造累积感，使暴力演变为可感知的过程。歌词以隐喻处理代际创伤、制度沉默与身体记忆，规避口号化的表达。整体呈现为一次关于生物、政治与历史压迫的节制研究，声音足够干净以暴露每一次冲击，同时保留足够的粗糙来维持不安。

items.album: Bringing down the walls of Jericho
items.excerpt: And when they make a long blast with the ram’s horn, when you hear the sound of the trumpet, then all the people shall shout with a great shout, and the wall of the city will fall down flat… -The Book Of Joshua, Chapter 6, Verse 5 Today we’re looking at two albums featuring saxophonists whose playing could bring down the walls of Jericho. Don Dietrich and Martin Escalante aren’t interested in melody in any ordinary sense of the term. You won’t find a cover of Surrey With The Fringe On Top here.
items.body: And when they make a long blast with the ram’s horn, when you hear the sound of the trumpet, then all the people shall shout with a great shout, and the wall of the city will fall down flat… -The Book Of Joshua, Chapter 6, Verse 5 Today we’re looking at two albums featuring saxophonists whose playing could bring down the walls of Jericho. Don Dietrich and Martin Escalante aren’t interested in melody in any ordinary sense of the term. You won’t find a cover of Surrey With The Fringe On Top here. They are living entirely on the very edge of what their instruments can do, skronking, screeching, howling, maybe a made-up verb with -ing on the end should go here. You won’t come away from these albums humming. But if you can find yourself in the same headspace as these musicians, you will come away from listening to this stunning, frequently shocking music exhilarated. Richard Cook and Brian Morton, in writing The Penguin Guide To Jazz, used the word “god-bothering” several times. I’m not sure they meant it as a compliment, but I take it as one. I frequently think of it when I listen to music like this. This music certainly isn’t for everyone, even among free jazz fans. But for those looking for extremity in their music, these albums are special. Dietrichs - Live Bahdu (Relative Pitch, 2026) First up is Live Bahdu by the Dietrichs. Don Dietrich, along with Jim Sauter and Donald Miller, formed the thunderous free jazz/harsh noise band Borbetomagus. Rather than sitting around trying to think of new adjectives to describe Borbetomagus, I would just urge you to check them out. They aren’t on Bandcamp, but there are many samples of their music on Youtube. (True story. I was once on a jazz open discussion group when someone wrote in asking for recommendations for music similar to Chuck Mangione. Some evil person who was not me, I swear, suggested Borbetomagus. I’ve often wondered what became of that poor listener.) Here we have Don joined by his daughter Camille Dietrich on cello. While this album has much of what you would expect from an album with Don Dietrich, Camille’s cello provides an exciting counterpoint to Don’s saxophone. She’s equally skilled at plucking and bowing, her classical music training brings moments of peace and musicality and then her desire to wreak musical mayhem takes over. Don responds and the result is some serious fire and brimstone. There’s a moment just before the 4-minute mark when there is some relative calm, and then the duo turns on a dime to create a shocking racket. The whole album is full of such surprises. Live Bahdu by Dietrichs Max Devereaux & Martin Escalante - Consequences Live! (Caresse Cassettes, 2026) And then there’s Martin Escalante. Another frequent creator of extreme sounds, Mats Gustafsson, said of Escalante: “This is the JAZZ we need! URGENT! DEDICATED! RADICAL! Unique-face-peeling-cutting-edge- and-totally-in-your-face-MF! This is ALL we need for a better living!” Who am I to argue with Mats Gustafsson, especially when he’s writing in ALL-CAPS? You might think Mats is exaggerating, but a listen to this album will tell you otherwise. Escalante, especially when he’s accompanied by a guitar, sounds punk as hell to me. I’m taken back to college days when I would crash off the walls of my dorm room screaming along to Black Flag. On this release he’s accompanied by the guitar of Max Devereaux, who manages to hold his own amid the noise and haste. He’s capable of creating his own ruckus but also quite good at providing accompaniment to Escalante on his wildest flights. At times he sounds like a rhythm section and at times he sounds like a machine gun. I wasn’t familiar with him before this album, and have been checking out his work since getting it. I hope to write more about him in the future. Consequences Live! by Max Devereaux & Martin Escalante Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook
items._cn_summary: 乐评聚焦两张2026年发行的极端自由爵士专辑。Dietrichs的《Live Bahdu》由前Borbetomagus成员Don Dietrich与女儿Camille Dietrich合作，萨克斯与古典训练背景的大提琴形成对话，在拨弦与拉弓之间切换，制造宁静与暴烈交替的张力，专辑中频繁出现突如其来的爆发转折。第二张Max Devereaux与Martin Escalante的《Consequences Live!》延续即兴萨克斯的极端探索路线。评论引用《约书亚记》耶利哥城墙倒塌的意象形容音乐冲击力，明确指出这些作品拒绝旋律可听性，致力于探索乐器表现的极限声音。两张专辑均由独立小厂牌发行，适合追求前卫听觉经验的听众。

items.artist: Dorothy Moskowitz & United States of Alchemy
items.excerpt:

items.body: Known for playing with County Joe McDonald, and for her experimental sound band The United States of America, Dorothy Moskowitz came back in 2023 with United States of Alchemy and their well-received release, Under an Endless Sky . In collaboration with avant-garde composer and filmmaker Francesco Paolo Paladino, and poet and music writer Luca Chino Ferrari, Songs of Compassion is eleven songs containing subversive and at times beautiful music, and richly evocative lyrics. Francesco Paolo Paladino and Luca Chino Ferrari | Photo by Maria Assunta Karini Songs of Compassion has two challenges for the listener. The first is the music, called variously avant-garde, ambient, modal, non-linear, and a few more. It is played mostly on pianos mixed in and out of the foreground, sometimes doubled, and sometimes out of phase, joined by strings, woodwinds, synth washes, and steely sounds. Initially disorienting, the music serves to remind us how locked our minds are to Western notions of harmonic movement. It speaks of alternative musical narratives much older and much further away. They are songs that subvert the song: more like Steve Reich than Steve Stills; more like Phillip Glass than Phil Collins. UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY - Pale Wanderer At the same time, there are the poetic yet strikingly contemporary lyrics. �Pale Wanderer� talks about the fact that authoritarianism needs willing accomplices, describing what happens �When you make a deal with darkness.� UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY (Dorothy Moskowitz, Francesco Paolo Paladino e Luka Chino Ferrari) by Silentes �Charlottesville� (written with the late Joe Byrd) evokes the time not long ago when torch-wielding nazis, proud of the metaphoric Ns on their tunics, chanted the antisemitic tropes paraphrased in Moskowitz�s words, �We�ll be one people, pure of race/No greedy throng could take our place� . Besides the overtly political lyrics, in the tradition of 1960s protest songs, there are also thoughtful meditations on mortality and our place in the universe. The message is high-minded yet sincere and direct. World weary and wise, Moskowitz�s voice inhabits the evocative philosophical lyrics with the authority of a skilled method actor. The melodies unfold like streams of consciousness, rising and falling, not following expected diatonic chord progressions, but honouring, instead, the value of each word. Moskowitz�s piano acts as another voice and sometimes a kind of Greek chorus commenting on the proceedings. The surrounding music frames, creates pulses and dissonances, and shimmers. The return of Dorothy Moskowitz with her renamed project has arrived in a moment quite similar to the times that spawned its predecessor. Political division, unrest, and uncertainty always generate artistic reaction, and United States of Alchemy roared back to life with their epic 24-minute opening track �Under an Endless Sky� in 2023, serving perhaps as an �In-A-Gadda-Da-Vida� for our times. Songs of Compassion continues to challenge how we think about our world. It�s music that defies the song form, while doing exactly what music is supposed to do�enrich the human condition. Find the artist online. The title track from the 2023 U.S. of Alchemy recording Under an Endless Sky by Dorothy Moskowitz & United States of Alchemy Further reading Cris Derksen - The Visit (Review) Tiny Sun - Vanishment (Review) Maria Ka - Di Mashin (Review) Further listening You will find a number of Dorothy Moskowitz's works on Race The Sky , most recently on Podgrammes #022 and #019.
items.label: Songs of Compassion
items._genre: avant-garde / experimental / contemporary classical / ambient / spoken word
items._cn_summary: 这张《Songs of Compassion》是Dorothy Moskowitz与作曲家Paladino、诗人Ferrari合作的专辑，共十一首歌曲。音乐以钢琴为核心，辅以弦乐、木管、合成器音色层叠与相位偏移处理，采用非线性和调式化手法，刻意摆脱西方和声进行逻辑，类似Steve Reich与Philip Glass的简约重复策略而非流行旋律。Moskowitz的演唱呈现世界性的疲惫与智慧，旋律随意识流起伏，钢琴如同希腊合唱队般对叙事进行评论。歌词兼具政治性与哲学性，延续六十年代抗议歌曲传统，涉及权威主义的合作机制、种族主义历史以及对死亡和宇宙位置的沉思。整体作品在实验音乐结构与社会议题文本之间形成持续张力，是一次对歌曲形式的系统性颠覆。

items.body: Kr�ta , the latest release on Norway's Taragot label, features a Swede and two Norwegians playing interpretations of mainly traditional tunes from their respective countries. Fiddler Mats Ed�n has long been involved in Swedish folk music, as a player, composer and teacher, and in the process exploring and integrating different musical styles and approaches. Tellef Kvifte was in the pioneering Norwegian crossover band Slinkombas in the 1970s and has continued to play a central role in Norwegian folk music, both as a musician and an academic. Most often heard playing the sj�fl�yte , more widely known as a recorder, Kvifte has employed other instruments from outside the Norwegian tradition, in particular the saxophone and bagpipes. His son Knut Kvifte Nesheim , a drummer and composer, has also shown a determination to blur the lines between different musical genres, both in his solo and group projects. Kr�ta by Ed�n/Kvifte/Nesheim trio It comes as no surprise then to find this trio offering a far from conventional take on the tunes they have chosen. While dance tunes may be the source of most of the material here, this feels more akin to chamber music; not that it is remotely classical in style, but in the sense it conveys of three players engrossed in a musically intimate conversation. This is not a performance appropriate for accompanying dancers but might instead be seen as an exploration of hidden possibilities of meaning in the music. In so doing it reveals some of its underlying mystery, including, perhaps, a darker side. Just as in an Ibsen play, where the surface bonhomie, jollity and social nicety can be hiding something more sinister, in Scandinavian dance music there are at times hints of a troublesome undercurrent below the surface. So the decision to open proceedings with �Fossgrimen,� a fiddle tune from Norway's Setesdal valley, is perhaps significant. A fossgrimen is a mythical creature, a kind of water-sprite living in waterfalls from whom fiddle-players were considered to have learned their skills and for that were not universally welcomed, with the fiddle considered to be the devil's instrument. Kr�ta by Ed�n/Kvifte/Nesheim trio Tellef Kvifte takes the lead melody on most tracks but on the Swedish �Polska from Per Myhr,� having played a repeated introductory riff on the sj�fl�yte, with Mats Ed�n providing an amorphous textural accompaniment below and Nesheim adding some quiet tinkling, it's Ed�n who introduces the tune on the fiddle with Kvifte proceeding to play in unison. It's a short track and almost as soon as it gets going things start to fragment and everything grind to a halt.

items.body: Sendas by Omar Sosa True to a Monk-inspired commitment never to play the same thing twice, Cuban pianist and composer Omar Sosa�s Sendas (Pathways), his latest solo offering, is the vivid invention of a pensive, restlessly creative, evolutionary artistry. As with all Sosa�s work, Sendas is the fortunate product of serendipity. In 2021 the COVID lockdown was underway, his marriage was ending, and a scheduled Milan appearance cancellation garnered an invitation to record at the Fazioli Pianoforti Concert Hall, annex to the renowned Italian piano manufactory in Sacile, Pordenone, about an hour northeast of Venice. At Fazioli, Sosa found himself in august company. Herbie Hancock and a host of classical pianists are Fazioli artists. Among the institutions that have embraced the Fazioli sound are the Juilliard School, Teatro La Fenice (Venice), the Budapest Palace of Arts, the Paris Conservatory, the Beijing Grand Theatre, and the universities of Salzburg, Graz, and Vienna. An unscripted two-hour solo improvisation on a Fazioli grand in the empty concert hall provided the raw audio for Sendas , later to be flavored in the mix, sparsely, with voice clips, percussion, loops, field recordings, found sounds effects that Sosa has collected over a career spanning four decades. As Sosa related to me soon after completing the post-production of Sendas , �Humanity is spiritually lost. We humans are all in this together. We need to evolve, but always keeping the traditions, walking with a strong, determined pace. We need more grounded music with overtones that resonate with the lower chakras� like throat singing, a mantra of the universal music.� �Creativity is about combining all your influences in a new way. I don�t aspire to be jazz, Latin, timba, reggaeton, classical. I avoid styles, but I respect the forms.� �I try not to think about how listeners will receive it but I do try to address their expectations, and go with the music to some other new place. Many free spirits come to listen, to be a part of the journey we are on.� Sosa laughs, �My son says, �Your niche is really small.� But the people who come really are there to be part of what we are going to do.� �Economics, technology, the streaming ear wash, algorithms all want to put you into a defined category � and so do many music journalists! The industry�s mentality is that any investment in artists must be defined by market categories to be profitable.� �But I play to be free of that,� Sosa says. �I play without thinking. There are no wrong notes. I love the first take. That�s the take, the natural voice of your soul. �Less is more� is a mantra in my life and music.� Consider the opening of �Inside the Spirit,� easing in leisurely, reaching over the keyboard into the resonant heart of the instrument, plucking and stroking the strings, teasing out a fuller resonance � only later to be embellished in the studio mix with light percussion and the muted Spanish-language refrain of a pregonero or street vendor, as might be heard in the calles of Havana or any other Latin American barrio. Sendas by Omar Sosa Moving from the secular to the sacred, �Deities Serenade� is an Afro-Cuban invocation of the shape-shifting divine, yet with ample room for ecumenical recasting in accord with a listener�s own self-location. �Inside My Soul� and �Something from Home� are Sosa works that to my ear may be an intuitive response to the distant call of Chopin�s "Nocturnes," to which Sosa says he listened every night for two years as a conservatory student in Cuba. Sendas by Omar Sosa �Caribbean Movement� and �Shirma� speak to Sosa�s rootedness in the lyrical, rhythmic, and harmonic heritage of the plantation islands where African and European cultures tragically entwined. In the violent forging of the world�s first truly modern people, social, cultural, linguistic, and musical displacements proved more flexible and accommodating than many of those same people, who shaped a contentious convergence of traditions into a changing same that persists into the unfolding present, ever yet to come. With expressive transcendence such as this, seeking to reduce the spiritual essence and inspiration of Sosa�s music to words is rather a fool�s errand. Better rather to listen, to contemplate, to perceive the pathway, to wander the sonic sendas coursing to the next way station without prejudice or preconception. To that end, Scott Price, Sosa�s longtime manager and friend relates, �We are using Sendas as the springboard for our first experiments in AI-generated Omar Sosa music videos.� Absent the opportunity to see and hear Sosa perform live, the palpable ideal, these ancillary audiovisual experiments further the ineffability of his artistic quest, the unique nature of the listening experience and all that ensues.

items._cn_summary: 古巴钢琴家 Omar Sosa 在意大利 Fazioli 音乐厅进行两小时无脚本独奏即兴录制，后期叠加人声采样、打击乐、循环音轨、田野录音和环境声响，形成多层次的声响拼贴。专辑诞生于疫情封锁与个人生活转折之际，Sosa 以冥想式的即兴手法探索钢琴的共鸣内核，引用 Monk 式'绝不复演'的创作信条，融合爵士即兴、拉美传统与世界音乐元素，并融入电子化后期处理。艺术家在访谈中表达对算法时代分类体系的抵抗，强调传统根基与精神共鸣的重要性，主张'少即是多'的极简美学。整体呈现出跨文化、跨类型的实验性独奏钢琴作品面貌。

items.body: With the completion of this trilogy, we acknowledge our part as a remote viewer of Dean’s life over three decades. Salvaging The Future—perhaps more than the prior two albums—is a restless collage, yet it is so well mixed that it lends itself to uninterrupted full-album listening. This listener is tuning in about 2x per day at the moment. Despite the challenges these decades have wrought, the trilogy’s close with “Our Story Survives Collectively” leaves us with a sense of hope. This is music for visioning. Revolutionizing the human listening experience Salvaging The Future by Dean De Benedictis Salvaging the Future utilizes electronic mastery alongside sparse traditional acoustic instruments and vocals to revolutionize the human listening experience. There will be no undisturbed sleeping, only optional vivid, deep-set dreaming. Music that completely upends your expectations can feel like a sensory assault on the first spin, but the feeling soon becomes mostly energizing and sustaining, including a wispy blend of limitless and beatless space signatures, as well as beat inspired enchantment. This is Art, intending to allow the unconscious mind to somehow express itself, often resulting in the depiction of illogical or dreamlike scenes and ideas. “Moving forward with mindfulness would quite literally mean salvaging the future,” offers De Benedictis. We may expect The Future to bring about profound changes in our listening arts through universal joyfulness, mindful that nothing is forever. As for dancing, that is up to you. I seek a collage shifting into every new world imaginable, or mostly never before imagined. Southern California-based artist Dean De Benedictis has delivered an absolute masterpiece for your collection of auditory journeys that completely bypass conventional reason and transport your mind into uncharted, supernatural territories. He ​is widely recognized in the electronic ambient community as Surface 10. Surface 10 has a long history with performing at galactic electronic music festivals as well as releasing his solo and collaborative recordings internationally, such as on the DiN label, Hypnotic, Space For Music, as well as some self-released works. His previous work with Spotted Peccary Music includes a collaborative project called Desensitized, with Deborah Martin (Hemispherica Portalis, 2020, and Chaos In Premonition, 2022) as well as two solo albums, Salvaging the Past (2005) and Salvaging the Present (2016). Only optional vivid, deep-set dreaming :: Salvaging the Future presents an attempt to conceive and apply a good degree of futurism to every aspect of its creation. From sound design, to instrumentation, to compositional production, perhaps one way to see it (or hear it) is as an illusive combination of progressive and contemporary influences that all “tap the future on the shoulder” or if nothing else, maybe exchange a hat-tip to that which is to come. Additionally, the obvious suggestion that humanity’s future may still have hope for survival and even thriving; that we may somehow redeem and persevere not by forgetting or dismissing our weight of the past, but acknowledging and accounting for life experiences as a strategy for our progress ahead. “Aside from representing phases of my life, the Salvaging series began as one idea, and ended as another,” confides De Benedictis. “The musical style of Salvaging The Future follows the suggestion of its inherent theme: a wild departure from most past and current genres, diving head first into hyper-forward approaches, perhaps in some ways “of the future.” “I would produce and perform music in harsh desert planes, steep canyons, mountainsides and summits, windswept shores and forested wilderness; I would work in abandoned buildings, housing construction, airplane flights, cafes, hotels, museums, libraries, or while staying with friends, family, or indeed at home, which was most of the time even if not by far. I tended to do a lot of re-synth types of methods, so found sounds combined with both customized sample libraries and Apple libraries were yet again the main source of instrumentation on Salvaging The Future, much like Salvaging The Present.” Also, like Salvaging The Present, there was an immense amount of processor stacking and automation, mountains of hardware, on every instrument track. “Featured on both albums was also a customized library of drum hits I created in 2014, in which each hit captures the reverb trail-from a note (or harmony) that was sung just before it. This hit library formulated a fairly unmistakable signature-sound in most of my work that followed. I still use that custom-drum-hits library to this day. However, unlike Salvaging The Present, which was completely produced on only one laptop, Salvaging The Future was composed on my first two laptops as well as my first tower. It was all old Apple gear and software, but for some reason that still sounded better to me than some of my newer gear and software, so I decided to just accept the old-system setbacks and finish the album on those devices regardless. A wild departure from most past and current genres :: “It almost broke me. I had to deal with endless system complications on every device, prompting constant work-arounds with Logic and Ableton, but the sound made it worthwhile for me.” De Benedictis continues his long, internationally recognized history of stripping ordinary objects of their normal significance to expose deep psychological truths. By tying an essential common thread between opposing genres, he has created an abstract, emotionally rich masterwork that demands to be heard for fans of avant-garde electronic exploration. Salvaging the Future was composed, performed, mixed, edited, designed and conceptualized by Dean De Benedictis between 2010 and 2025, using mostly software on laptops. His additional instruments were flute, voice, piano and guitar. Production locations were scattered throughout the US west coast but based primarily in Thousand Oaks and Santa Monica, CA. Contributing extra recorded musicians, in addition to Apple loops, include: Lara De Benedictis (vocals), D’Von Charley (vocals and native flute), Nichole Michelle Jones (vocals), Lisa Claire Mitterer (vocals), Phil Williams (electric guitar), and various ASMR artists. ASMRtists. Autonomous Sensory Meridian Response (ASMR) and Ray Kersweil’s futurist theory of the Singularity are two unrelated ideas I came across while researching this music, both have been popular but I have never before heard of them, so kudos. ASMR seems to explore some of the physical psychology of sound. The Kersweil concepts are set in the future, during the coming singularity, and all planets and celestial bodies are now shifting and morphing and changing as that same singularity. This revolutionary sonic journey begins abruptly with “My Love Is An Extinction Event” (6:10), a track whose song title invokes the concept of a rapid, widespread drop in biodiversity. Here things come together and things come apart and sometimes this happens at the same time, spinning and bouncing, falling and transferring velocity, which feels bizarre, unbelievable, dreamlike and leads into very strange restless ear-born images. The kind that will change your life. At one moment the mood goes from feeling frenetic to feeling incredibly alive and layered. This unexpected salad of situations, places, or emotional moments that seem detached from everyday reality or logic all feel pretty good, the intimate links between freeing imagination and the mind, and liberation from repressive and archaic social structures. In the beginning, deep space has no beat. Welcome to “The Outer Links”  (6:31). Coming from an intentionally beatless expanse designed to liberate the imagination, giving the listener the sensation of flying through colorful lights, and maneuvering deliberately to liberate the imagination. We are flying along at a more rapid speed now. The feeling is all about bright stars and a sense of transit. Soon everything is almost flying apart and the beat is going at a fast clip. As the album progresses, we encounter “Voca”  (3:35), where small pieces suddenly click and morph into a fast-paced, jamming run driven by a sexy bassline and seasonably hot drum tones. Perhaps the tempo is a bit fidgety but always rich in tone and interesting in context, jumping into many places to tell the story. I do not understand the punchline, but even real life itself can be strange and even uncomfortable when seeking sustenance. Music for visioning :: I think the fourth track starts in a calm memory palace illuminated with tall marble columns, with big bright halls and stairways. Soon a beat contraption comes together and the vocalists start to arrive. “They Fought To Sway” (7:18) is my personal favorite here, the vocals reach a place I have never heard before, and I like that. “Urband Glacier Fund”  (6:27) is probably holding a hidden message, leading to speculation about that extra d in Urband. Hidden portals bring delight, I think that we are in outer space coming upon some new life forms, our synthesizers are carefully subtle and fully capable. Now a new beat arrives and takes over, a new darkness has surrounded the cabin. Are there glaciers in outer space? The flute is here to take us along, with amazing high energy. Now we encounter a big cinematic sly beat and things are happening all over the place, very exciting. “ASMR Tragedy Lines” (6:44) seems to take place down in a very deep tunnel or cavern, robots are building things quietly, except for this one guy. It gets extremely quiet out here, where we are in the cavern. The perception distorts, morphs, and transforms ordinary objects and forms into strange and uncanny variations of themselves. Down there something is always sparkling. Now the whispers in the darkness take over. I keep straining to hear what the voices are planning next. The imaginary narrative shifts beautifully on “Salvaging My Story” (7:12), a track full of radiant stars, choirs, and unexpected juxtapositions that exercise the grand element of surprise. Let’s go out into the fields at night where the space ships will land, be sure to keep an eye out. There are steam powered machines running, there are crickets and I expect to find the children of the night out here. Soon there is a change. There is a shy melodic tune lingering in the caverns along with the choirs and radiant stars. Soon all of the details start coming into focus, this is a big story with plenty of flying at night. Away we are going, exercising the element of surprise, unexpected juxtapositions and non sequitur. It works. This leads right into the slow-burning sunrise of “Future Incandescence” (6:32) which unfolds like a long slow transit in deep space. Now the pace is slower and the feeling is starker, disorienting, with the hallucinatory quality of a dream. There is a language of fragments that flow together and make the whole sound. We are still on the ship, snug inside a safe metal box that is still moving, the closest star is emerging from an eclipse, there are emotions and suspense, there is tension building. The natural world takes a surreal turn on “All The Wild” (4:27), where there are strange gumblings coming from animals that I cannot see. We are all probably back in the big cave again, at night. This time with strange recordings of birds and wildlife playing in the darkness. The variety of strange sounds increases as new species come floating into our range. There are a lot of creatures heard here, such as birds or lizards cooing, insects clicking and humming. I think I hear a synth glowing, perhaps a swan, with pianos and choirs and sustained tones echoing about. Some loons explode or just fly ahead, and there are more new strange creatures. There are whales in our cave here, along with the strings and wings. “Born Of Flight” (7:09) starts in quiet secrecy before combusting into a galloping drum kit that soon clicks like a flying train, keeping the listener in a state of perpetual, blissful motion. We love our cave, it goes on forever. By the end we are clicking like a sleeping railroad carriage, always feeling motion, until we gently float into the close. The album concludes with a magnificent nine-minute epic, “Our Story Survives Collectively” (9:15), and to start we are following our guide into the well lit tunnel or hallway, there are echoes and lots of space above. There are interesting odd vocals, some with a trilling vibrato. Now for me there was suddenly a grand design to the whole program. I could see that there are complimentary combinations of elements and a thriving life force, and we are all together. Salvaging The Future by Dean De Benedictis   Dean De Benedictis is a Southern California-based artist who has always utilized his interest in a variety of styles and cultures to enrich the quality of his musical expression. He aspires to communicate a similar functionality for the experiences of his listeners. Deans’ music is the result of his will to tie an essential common thread together between opposing genres and mentalities, as well as draw from them a natural sense of emotion, expanse and mystery. Sound exposes psychological truth; stripping ordinary objects of their normal significance, to create a compelling image that is beyond ordinary formal organization, in order to evoke empathy from the listener, with a combination of the depictive, the abstract, and the psychological.Driving into the complex, shape-shifting worlds that De Benedictis creates is always a magnificent adventure. He juxtaposes those frantic, glitchy granular textures against massive, cinematic spaces, sometimes he drops a rogue flute solo or harmonica right into a heavy electronic beat. It’s the kind of music that feels less like a collection of songs and more like a living, breathing, possibly dangerous ecosystem; De Benedictis has created an abstract, emotionally rich soundscape universe that rewards the listener.“My Salvaging trilogy of albums was a sincere and perhaps far-flung attempt to tie a form of common thread between the periods of my life and the electronic music I never released during those periods. Naturally, the reoccurring concept and eventual theme of ‘salvaging time’ manifested into the project. I basically have boxes filled with music like this, built up through decades. As such, my Salvaging trilogy was only one of many projects with a similar goal – to salvage works of the past – but the Salvaging Trilogy itself might be my most qualitative among them.“There are some very clear differences in style and approach contrasting each of these three albums, but it’s really the difference between the first album and the two albums following that one where the contrast is most visible. My first Salvaging album in 2005, Salvaging The Past, was a collection of work created throughout the ‘90s in my home studio, where I was surrounded by physical synthesizers and racks of outboard gear. Sometime between that album and the next one, Salvaging The Present, I acquired my first laptop and lots of appropriate software (more laptops would soon follow).“This changed the game, and my life, in ways that I couldn’t have imagined years earlier. I was already a traveler and an outdoorsman, so suddenly having the power to virtually access an entire studio within a little portable box was very liberating, conceptually and literally. I ended up travelling far and wide with the music, albeit mostly within US borders, but still found myself creating spontaneous productions in some of America’s most extreme natural environments. Over a period of about a decade-and-a-half, I lived a separate little lifetime of fair adventure with these devices, even including some uncomfortable brushes with death.“This spanned the length of both concurrent albums after the first one, I endured to keep creating through massive amounts of life changes and personal upheaval; through each new home I found, whether on-the-road or stationary; through broken alliances and rock-and-jazz-band breakups; through family drama and harddrive thefts and accidental overdoses, and of course a pandemic. Even through it all, my personal standard of innovation-balanced-by-emotional-sincerity never faltered, which probably explains the long lapses between Salvaging albums.“My desire to musically attempt going where no man or woman had gone before, both sonically and musically, remained. Everything from my sound-design methods to my processing methods to my performing and editing methods, was all totally signature, through every twist and turn and every new resolution. I suppose that’s what’s most noticeable and even distinguishable about this last and final album of the trilogy, Salvaging The Future; it’s the one with the biggest complexities and most contrasting styles, because my desire for balance between cutting-edge method and emotional sincerity were still unwavering through even the most tumultuous period of my life.”It is only natural, after all, to keep pace with scientific and industrial progress as well as follow the lure of pure psychic automatism, to stand for transforming the alienation which many people feel in the modern period, combined with the sense of reaching more deeply into the psyche, to be made whole with one’s individuality.With the completion of this trilogy, we acknowledge our part as a remote viewer of Dean’s life over three decades. Salvaging The Future—perhaps more than the prior two albums—is a restless collage, yet it is so well mixed that it lends itself to uninterrupted full-album listening. This listener is tuning in about 2x per day at the moment. Despite the challenges these decades have wrought, the trilogy’s close with “Our Story Survives Collectively” leaves us with a sense of hope. This is music for visioning. Salvaging The Future is available on Spotted Peccary Music. [Bandcamp] Salvaging The Future by Dean De Benedictis  The post Dean De Benedictis :: Salvaging The Future (Spotted Peccary Music) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.
items._cn_summary: Dean De Benedictis 完成其"救赎三部曲"终章，以电子技法为核心，辅以稀疏的原声乐器与人声，营造出不断切换的拼贴式声景。评论指出专辑适合不间断地整张聆听，融合了无节拍的太空氛围与节拍驱动的迷幻段落，试图将未来主义理念贯穿于声音设计、编曲与制作全过程。作品不追求连贯叙事，而是以碎片化的画面感激发听者的潜意识联想，尾声曲目传递出集体叙事延续的希望感。艺术家此前以 Surface 10 之名活跃于电子氛围场景，曾与厂牌 DiN、Spotted Peccary 合作多个项目，专辑在小型独立厂牌发行，整体定位偏向实验性氛围音乐而非商业制作。

items.excerpt: By the time Syna Awel reaches “Incantation”, the sun has dropped. It closes an open-air acoustic session she filmed in a single afternoon this year, five Amazigh songs in a row, the last easing into a jam as the daylight goes. She is Franco-Algerian, a singer and percussionist who grew up in Aït Bouaddou, a village in the Kabyle mountains of northern Algeria. Her songs come out of Amazigh oral tradition, poetry and melody carried by voice, and she brings them into contemporary jazz.
items.body: By the time Syna Awel reaches “Incantation”, the sun has dropped. It closes an open-air acoustic session she filmed in a single afternoon this year, five Amazigh songs in a row, the last easing into a jam as the daylight goes. She is Franco-Algerian, a singer and percussionist who grew up in Aït Bouaddou, a village in the Kabyle mountains of northern Algeria. Her songs come out of Amazigh oral tradition, poetry and melody carried by voice, and she brings them into contemporary jazz. For the session she sings with Luc Lavenne on guitar, Anis Agrebi on oud, Tony Sgro on derbouka and Mahir Bostandzija on percussion. Where the album set her voice against jazz piano and bendir, this acoustic line-up answers with oud and hand percussion. Awel sings “Incantation” in Kabyle. The line “Kul yiwen yesɛa tidet-ines” means everyone holds their own truth, and the next line adds that everyone does what they can. She sets that against the turning of a day: the sun sets, the moon takes the evening, and it all comes round again. The songs come from Awel, her 2024 debut, arranged by drummer Karim Ziad and released on Imago Records. The full session, subtitled in Kabyle and French, plays on her YouTube channel. items.body:
One of electronic music's most influential recordings, back in circulation.

Most readers of these pages will know the story, but to indulge you with a recap, Gottsching was part of electronic krautrock heroes Ash Ra Tempel and in 1981, off the back of a Klaus Schulze tour, sat down one evening and dropped a continuous piece of music which would uncannily imagine the arc of dance music for a quarter of a century.

Early adopters in the Chicago and Detroit warehouses and mediterranean pleasure palaces must have thrilled to the balanced and continuous surging flow of the hour long piece - even over two sides the mix is perfect for building a club atmosphere and suggesting avenues for mixing, whilst using merely two chords throughout. the minimalism offsets the percussive splendour perfectly - several years later the tune was rediscovered and co-opted into the huge italo house smash Sueno Latino, which cemented its foundation in the burgeoning balearic scene of the time and proceeded through several spells of rapturous revival throughout the nineties, not least when figures like Carl Craig and Basic Channel issued their own radically different reshapes and remakes of the piece.

Very satisfying then to have this Gottsching sanctioned edition, where the game might truly be said to have begun in earnest. As they say on the august walls of the Hardwax emporium - buy or die.
items._cn_summary: 曼努埃尔·格青1981年在一个夜晚创作了这张长达一小时的连续电子音乐作品，仅用两个和弦贯穿始终，却预示了未来二十五年舞曲发展的走向。专辑以极简主义手法构建持续涌动的节奏律动，完美适合俱乐部混音氛围。克雷格与Basic Channel等底特律 techno 先驱后来均以此为素材进行重塑，意大利 house 经典《Sueno Latino》也采样了此作。克青本人授权的版本重新进入流通领域，作为电子音乐史上一件具有开创性意义的录音，其影响跨越德国 krautrock、芝加哥 house、底特律 techno 与地中海 balearic 多个场景，奠定了极简电子舞曲的美学范式。

items.body:
On her third studio album, Brooklyn-based artist Frances Chang feels out the boundary between bedroom pop and lavishly orchestrated avant-experimentation, writing on a century-old grand piano and spiking her productions with jerky, unconventional electronic elements. The end result is somewhere between Aimee Mann and Cate Le Bon.

There's something unmistakably ramshackle about Chang's productions, but at the same time, it all sounds as if it's been meticulously planned. On opening track 'I can feel the waves', her voice never falters as it soars over casual phrases from her aging baby grand, but the it's the beats that immediately catch your attention, rupturing the calm with the momentum of a footwork demo. Chang's clearly an obsessive listener and it's this passion that lends her songs a breath of originality; they're classic in a sense, informed by Burt Bacharach, Chet Baker and Dionne Warwick, which actually makes sense. And where she takes the songs after they've been written is fascinating, building them out with instrumentation that's not exactly unexpected, it's just ever so slightly off-kilter. Those warbling strings on the ace 'Bad zen', or the buzzing micro-repetitions on 'Marry' - these sounds just nudge the material into a different zone and assert Chang's personality.

And as it develops, Chang's confidence grows. She's most successful when the guardrails are fully off - like on the brilliant 'No avatar'. Here, she latches her Robert Ashley-esque vocal lead to a wonky synth arpeggio that she follows with piano - or vice versa? The other instruments coolly fall into line: drums, bass and organ seem to flutter, flourish and fall at Chang's command, never quite going in the expected direction. Even advance single 'Auratones of Desire' makes more sense in context, its well-sculpted fusion of psych drum breaks, frittered farfisa organs and soft vocal affectations widening the album's reach considerably. Given it some time and attention for full reward.
items._genre: avant-pop / experimental / bedroom pop / electronic / singer-songwriter
items._cn_summary: Frances Chang的第三张专辑在卧室流行与华丽管弦乐式前卫实验之间游走。她以一架有百年历史的三角钢琴为写作核心，却在制作中混入节奏突兀的电子节拍与footwork式律动。人声稳健从容地漂浮于不规则的钢琴织体之上，弦乐颤音、微型循环嗡鸣以及失谐的合成器琶音将歌曲推向意料之外的声场。整张作品呈现出精心策划的即兴感，传统songwriting骨架（Bacharach、Baker、Warwick的影响）与后现代拼贴并置。从开篇人声与节拍的撕裂，到中后段管风琴、psychedelic鼓击与软化唱腔的融合，专辑的叙事弧线随制作手法的愈发自信而逐渐打开，需要反复聆听方可充分接收其细节。

items.body:
Daria Lourd (Bored Lord) + her wife, vocalist Jaelynn Walls = DARLYNN on their debut shot of Jersey club meets ‘90s R&B, woozy garage house and vintage psych-funk flavours.

"Darlynn is an Oakland-based duo composed of Daria Lourd (aka Bored Lord) and her wife, vocalist Jaelynn Walls. Dyke Den is a lesbian love story about two creative individuals finding each other and themselves through effusive and contemplative sonic avenues. Created in their home over the course of two years, this album speaks to the journey of Daria and Jaelynn’s romantic relationship as well as their evolving combined creative impulses.

On Dyke Den, Darlynn display their influences – from Janet Jackson and Sly & the Family Stone, to Frankie Knuckles and Larry Levan – in a sophisticated, fully realized, and overtly queered fashion. Joyous dancefloor moments are abundant. Tracks like “Make Yr Move” and “Like A Summer” celebrate deep house vibes ala Alleviated Records, while sultry R&B moves are flexed on “Girl 2 Girl” and “Alright With Me.” But longing and yearning exist within this joyous arc, and the question arises: “How can I get you to love me?” More than an idealistic narrative of girl meets they/them, Dyke Den paints a portrait of love in all its multifaceted moments: the bids for commitment, the stagnation of years going by, the wormholes of desire. Yet the album maintains its thesis of hope. The sweet, layered harmonies of closing song “Love Letter” display the power of life partnership: “My whole life is a love letter to you.” Dyke Den features artwork by Hailee Va in a sleeve designed by Eloise Shir-Juen Leigh. Darlynn’s final declaration, “We are all creatures of desire, completely built for love.”s"

items._cn_summary: Darlynn是由Daria Lourd（又名Bored Lord）与妻子Jaelynn Walls组成的奥克兰双人组。这张专辑以女同性恋爱情故事为主线，记录了两人在家庭录音室中两年间的共同创作与情感历程。音乐上融合了Jersey club节奏、90年代R&B、迷幻车库浩室与复古放克元素，既有适合舞池的欢快节拍，也有慵懒性感的R&B时刻，并穿插对渴望与承诺的沉思。受Janet Jackson、Sly & the Family Stone、Frankie Knuckles等影响，作品以成熟而鲜明的酷儿视角重新诠释这些经典声音。结尾曲《Love Letter》以层层叠叠的和声表达伴侣关系的力量，为整张专辑赋予希望与爱的主题。

items.body:
Michael J. Blood lends two rugged, tumping takes to Intertoto’s rudely groggy beatdown house

‘If I Take You Home’ is the first cut from London’s Intertoto since his well received album ‘Thermal Shadow’ (2023) and continues down a midnight path of mid-tempo, strutting beatdown roughly guided by likes of NWAQ and Kassel Mosse.

MJB steps it up a gear or two in a ‘Walk of Shame Mix’ built from woodcut kicks and gritty sampler revs plus additional vox like Martin Rev just walked in the room and did a Travolta “huh?”, plus a banging ‘Morning After Mix’ cloaked in muffled party noise and prompting jelly legs back to the ‘floor.
items._cn_summary: Intertoto 在《Thermal Shadow》之后推出首支单曲《If I Take You Home》，延续其中速午夜风格的 beatdown house 路线，受到 NWAQ 与 Kassel Mosse 等艺术家的影响。Michael J. Blood 为这首作品提供了两个混音版本：Walk of Shame Mix 以木质击打感的鼓点和粗粝的采样推进，并加入类似 Martin Rev 式的人声插段；Morning After Mix 则包裹在模糊的派对噪音中，营造出令人腿软重返舞池的律动。整体上，这张混音单曲在舞曲框架内强调质感与氛围，带有明显的实验倾向，适合关注地下电子场景的听众。

items.body:
Kurt Wagner's seventeeth album as Lambchop - drawing on gospel and centuries-old Scots-Appalachian call-and-response singing.

"Lambchop's seventeenth album Punching the Clown finds Kurt Wagner returning to first principles. Sparked by a late-night radio encounter with an unidentified gospel recording, Wagner fell deep into the world of "lined out singing" a centuries-old Scots-Appalachian call-and-response tradition in which a lone clerk leads a choir through hymns, word by unadorned word. That spirit of raw, communal voice shapes every moment of Punching the Clown: Wagner spent years studying great songwriters and relearning his craft from the ground up, whittling dozens of songs down to twelve. Recorded in three days with guitarist Andrew Broder, Justin Vernon on banjo, and a six-part choir assembled by Blake Morgan and engineered by Lambchop veteran Mark Nevers, the album is graceful, wry, and quietly devastating. Out August 21, 2026 on City Slang.

Produced by Ryan Olson and recorded August 25–27, 2025, at April Base, Wisconsin. The record was completed over three days and features Kurt Wagner (vocals), Andrew Broder (guitar), Justin Vernon (banjo), and a six-part vocal ensemble, with additional choir recordings in London and Minneapolis."
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是Lambchop主脑Kurt Wagner回归本源之作。受深夜电台中一段无名福音录音启发，他深入研究了“lined out singing”这一古老的苏格兰-阿巴拉契亚呼应歌唱传统，由领唱者逐字引导合唱团回应。Wagner花费数年研习伟大词曲作者并重新打磨创作，将数十首作品精简为十二首。专辑在三天内录制完成，吉他手Andrew Broder、班卓琴手Justin Vernon以及六人合唱团共同参与，制作人Ryan Olson与长期合作的Mark Nevers也贡献其中。整体呈现优雅、诙谐而沉静的质感，人声的质朴与合唱的共同体感成为核心，在极简编排中透出克制的力量。

items.body:
Showcasing contemporary Algerian sounds led by the gasba, a traditional reeded flute, 'My Heart is Dust Before Him' is a collaboration between Hive Mind and Oran's Édition Ahlem imprint.

In the Berber language, "gaspa" means "reed", and references the wind instrument that's central to some of the region's most gripping Bedouin folk and ceremonial music. On this 10-track anthology, Hive Mind plucks tracks from Édition Ahlem's recent catalogue; the label emerged in Oran from a record store and puts out cassettes since the early '90s. These selections are a little more contemporary and examine how the gasba forms have mutated and evolved in the last couple of decades, reacting to production changes while retaining the unique sound of the flute itself.

There's plenty to explore here, from the dimly lit distortions of Cheikh Tahar Oueld Marhoum's 'Naachak Fiha Ou Magoulhach' and Cheba Negouane's rai-adjacent 'Ychafouni Maghbounat' to Cheikh El Waal's woozy organ-led 'El Galb Maamar' and Mohamed Ain Larbaa's unexpectedly funky 'Sratli Khatra Kheleft L3ahed'.
items._genre: world music / folk / experimental / traditional fusion
items._cn_summary: 这张合辑聚焦阿尔及利亚传统乐器gasba（芦苇笛）在当代语境下的演变，由Hive Mind与奥兰独立厂牌Édition Ahlem合作推出。Édition Ahlem自上世纪九十年代初便以磁带形式发行本地音乐，合辑从中精选十首曲目，展示了gasba如何在保留其独特音色与游牧/仪式音乐根基的同时，对制作方式的变化做出回应。曲目跨越多种风格取向：从Cheikh Tahar Oueld Marhoum暗哑失真的处理，到Cheiba Negouane贴近rai的演绎，再到Cheikh El Waal以管风琴领引的迷幻氛围，以及Mohamed Ain Larbaa出人意料的放克律动。这些作品既非纯粹的民俗录音，也非西方实验框架下的拼贴，而是gasba作为核心乐器在不同编曲逻辑下的当代延伸，对于关注非西方音乐传统如何被重新诠释的听众而言，是一份值得细听的资料。
