items.body:
Necessary reissue of Marc Leclair’s immaculate Y2K micro-house/dub-house 12” as Akufen, dispensed by Low End Activist’s guess-again BRUK sibling to Sneaker Social Club - huge RIYL Maurizio, Studio 1, Mike Huckaby.

‘Architextures 1 -2 -3’ is a sought-after slice of hypnotic house by a noted pioneer of the micro-house movement that emerged in the late ‘90s. Its reissue arrives in the wake of a re-up for Marc Leclair’s (aka Akufen) sole solo album ‘Musique Pour 3 Femmes Enceintes’ (2005) with a strong reminder of his pivotal role in dressing house music down to fundamentals around the millennium, as deployed in Richie Hawtin mixes and praised for its exquisitely efficient, effortless, hiccuping funk.

It’s really all about the  A-side’s ‘Architexture 1’, a pendulous 127BPM roller inflected with chef’s kiss dub chords and frisky drums, on one of the smoothest, deepest basslines since ‘M5’. There’s a good reason why it’s been fetching triple figures on 2nd hand markets, so BRUK are doing the Lord’s work with this reissue, which also includes the slower, sub-heavier swivel of its Pt. 2, and more signature, strutting clip of his tight sampling tekkerz on Pt. 3.

TIP!
items._cn_summary: Akufen（本名Marc Leclair）是九十年代末微缩house运动的重要先驱，这张重新发行的EP收录了其标志性的极简house作品。A面的'Architexture 1'以127BPM的摇摆节奏为核心，融合dub和弦与灵动鼓点，低音线深沉流畅，可与Maurizio经典'M5'相媲美。整张作品展现了将house音乐精简至骨骼的功力——碎片化采样与hiccup式律动构成独特的微观声响美学，曾在Richie Hawtin的混音集中被广泛运用。B面与第三轨延续了这种采样驱动的技术风格，节奏更慢更沉。三曲连听可见Akufen对house结构性拆解的持续探索，是理解千禧年前后极简电子美学脉络的重要文献。

items.body:
Limited edition, first time 2LP re-issue of a compilation originally released via Gary Mundy's legendary Broken Flag imprint in 1987 and featuring a veritable who’s who of post industrial drone and psyche/power electronics including Ramleh, Total, Andrew Chalk and many more.​

"Remastered by Puppy38, this features two bonus tracks not included on the original (and long o/p) LP but only previously found on the even rarer cassette and the equally o/p CD. A timely reminder of this fantastic archive document full of boundary-pushing artists mostly still active in one form or another. Packaged in a sleeve faithful to the distinctive original Cranioclast-designed cover."
items._genre: industrial / power electronics / drone / noise / post-industrial
items._cn_summary: 这是1987年由Gary Mundy旗下传奇厂牌Broken Flag首次发行的合辑首次2LP再版限量发行，汇集了Ramleh、Total、Andrew Chalk等后工业嗡鸣与心能电子领域的核心人物。Puppy38负责重新母带处理，再版收录了两首原始黑胶未收但曾出现在更稀有的磁带与CD版本中的bonus曲目。封面由Cranioclast设计，忠实还原了原版独特的视觉风格。这份档案文献记录了当年突破边界的声音实践，多数参演艺术家至今仍以不同形式活跃于地下场景，对工业与极端声响领域的研究者与收藏者而言具有重要的历史参考价值。

items.body: Left: P+D 02 01 02 (2024); Right: M P Landis & Michael Sarin, May 18, 2024 at L/A Arts, Lewiston, ME Adjacent to a drumkit, two large boards hang above a stage clad in drop cloth. A third lies flat on a small table surrounded by paint bottles and upturned pot lids that will become ad hoc palettes. Each board is covered in paper and divided into grids by white painter's tape: the small board into nine squares and the larger two into twelve. It's the end of June 2026 at the Apohadion Theater in Portland, Maine. Just ahead, the fifth meeting of painter M P Landis and drummer Michael Sarin in a collaboration they've come to call, concisely, Paint & Drums. Fans of creative music may recognize Landis's paintings from the album covers of artists like Flow Trio , [ism] , and Sabir Mateen . His work is part of an estuary somewhere far downstream of the Abstract Expressionists: gestures that range from child-like markings to purposive strokes that convey the whole body's movement; textured clots and layers of color; obscure figures and shapes that could be letters or symbols but offer a mute refusal. But Landis will say he feels less affinity with other visual artists than he does with musicians. Indeed, what stands out about Landis's work is how deeply committed his methods are to the same reactive, exuberant ethos that drives the free improvisers. Music—especially jazz and improvised music—has long been part of Landis's work, both in the studio and in a live setting. In a 2006 conversation with the writer Fred Schmalz, he described arriving at a point in the 1990s where he began using music "as a jumping off point to get beyond my ideas and find a way of working that transcends technique and becomes more emotional and dance-like." Joe Maneri/Mat Maneri/Randy Peterson #1 - #4 (2001). Created live at the 2001 Vision Festival, NYC His career in the decades since validates Mike Heffley's musing in Northern Sun, Southern Moon. "If one were a painter," Heffley wrote, free improvisation "is music that might be the most fruitful aid and stimulus to the process. It encourages one to get physical with one's tools and media, to delight in them as ends in themselves, whatever means they might develop into therefrom." Talking with Schmalz, Landis describes exactly that: "I feel almost like the music uses me or, I guess I use the music to use me. There is a certain surrendering to what I am listening to which helps me jump right into physically moving; making marks, grabbing paint, etc. It overcomes the endless problems of decision and throws me right into the act of creating." Some of Landis's paintings bear titles that pay tribute to the music he was listening to as he painted. But music's influence is more deeply seated. Top: David S. Ware: Onecept triptych (mp13.01, mp13.02, mp13.03) (2013) Bottom Left: PIANO SKY (JOE MANERI) (2003); Bottom Right: lp13.06 (derek bailey) (2013) Landis moved from painting on street corners and in the audience at concerts to frequently painting on stage in collaboration with musicians, dancers, and other visual artists in the vibrant Brooklyn arts scene. He remains a prolific collaborator. The live performances of that period culminated in a tour with the Jump Arts American Road Project in 2002, Landis taking the stage with poet Steve Dalachinsky, dancers, and musicians like Tom Abbs, Daniel Carter, Steve Swell, and Okkyung Lee. Cisco Bradley's recounting of the tour in The Williamsburg Avant-Garde touches on Landis's intense engagement with his materials and an approach to live painting that's still present in Paint & Drums: "[Landis] would paint through the entire evening of performances, with two wooden panels covered in paper on which to work. One panel was covered by one large piece of paper, while the other panel had multiple smaller pieces stapled to it. Landis described his process: 'I painted the whole board, not thinking about where one piece of paper stopped or started. I liked how it gave the work a sense of being midstream, like capturing a sound in time.' He added, 'The intensity of the music made the painting intense. It felt like I was doing months' worth of painting within a few hours.'" Left: american road project 1L (2002); Right: j.a.a.r.p. [#12.] (2002) It was during his time in NYC that Landis met Sarin, then drumming in the storied Thomas Chapin Trio (just one facet of his deep and continued embeddedness in the New York avant-garde). Nearly two decades later, Sarin lamented that he never had a chance to see Landis paint in a live setting and asked if he'd be willing to collaborate. Two performances were arranged in May 2024, and the duo have now met three more times in 2026. A Visual Musician There's an enticing trap, or at least a long stroll to a dead end, in approaching the relationship between Landis's paintings and free jazz. It is to interpret them as somehow "representing" the music. Landis is clear on this: "I don’t mean for [the music] to define the work because I’m not interested in making visual representations of music, or anything for that matter. These paintings and drawings are artifacts of a creative process; a recording of my reactions to not just music, but to life and my living it." Establishing that the relationship is indirect, two smaller traps await, both common responses to abstract music and painting. Treading carefully between them, I'm likely to get a foot caught in each. The first comes from the dismissive "Even I Could Have Done That" school of art criticism; the other adopts a transcendental tone that inflates the abstract nature of these artforms until they're lofted into the clouds. Something like "overwhelming directness" versus "overweening mystery," to borrow from Stanley Cavell. Left to Right: MONK 3. THINK OF ONE (2005); MONK 4. HACKENSACK (2005); MONK 5. 'ROUND MIDNIGHT (2005) The first response is an almost defensive tensing in the face of such directness. A move to immediately let the air out before the overweeners get too jazzed up. "I get it. Your painting is like free jazz: random and improvised and spontaneous." Nothing enigmatic here. You don't really have to know anything, you just have to do. Splatter the paint, whack the drum, toot the horn. This attitude tends to badly underestimate the skill that's required to achieve the allegedly facile result, but there's something perceived here, a focus on the plain fact of bodies in action, that can't be entirely dismissed. The process, the doing, is integral—it's what's insisted by these artforms, what we can always sense even when we try (willfully or otherwise) to bracket it out. In viewing pieces like the "Monk Work" paintings, those initial impressions of sheer spontaneity belie the fact that, just as in lots of jazz and improvised music, accumulated experience and an incredible depth of consideration are channeled into an application of skill, shaping an ongoing process that didn't have a specific end in mind when things got underway. What get overlooked are all the particularities: the whorl of circumstance, body, and action that actually birthed that painting or moment of music. Landis's painting isn't merely like free jazz because both can be loud and break rules. Many of his pieces represent a series of events and decisions through time—sometimes over weeks and months—that are fervently attuned to intention and accident and their intertwining. Left : 16.35T (2016); Right : 19.155 (2019) We often fall back on visual metaphors when trying to talk about music, but the counterintuitive thing about Landis's paintings is that their material likeness to music is not visual, but temporal: they are "impossible" images that inscribe action-through-time in the same way that music does as it plays out. This sense of movement-across-time leaps from their surfaces. Looking at a piece like 16.35T , I really do find myself reaching for musical concepts: there's a staccato rhythm to the marks, which have a lively motion in their stacks of contrapuntal bands. There's dissonance in the dabs of glowing green, which seem to punctuate moments in the painting's development. The paintings have no telos, just as improvised music isn't about getting to the end of playing. They aren't planned and realized ends or even a representation of an instant or "the now" but rather they are a holding-open, a paradoxical attempt to spatialize temporality, or express it all at once. The time-taking is the work in the way music is the running of the clock. This temporal nature is never more apparent than during live performance. There, we see the changing cadences of painting, the transformation of color and form as new strokes merge with old, the accumulation of layers that continually supplant the painting's character, even as glimpses of its previous features remain. Brice Marden once said of Jackson Pollock, "He doesn't apply the image; he lets the image evolve out of the activity." Landis: "I like to push what I make ‘til it feels right, in some inner logic kind of way, even when that leads me to something that might look off or clumsy, but in a way that attracts me." All of these evolved and evolving particularities are exactly why just anyone couldn't create that painting or improvise those sounds. Those unrepeatable elements in concert with the artist's grappling are what constitute the work. If such painting or music could be said to have "content," this is all it could possibly be, and encrypted. You may be physically capable of executing the work, but you could never be existentially capable—you have no access to its means of creation. Top, Left to Right: wd3060 (2006); wd2034 (2004); wd5625 (2013) Middle, Left to Right: wd5921 (2014); wd6016 (2014); wd6058 (2014) Bottom, Left to Right: wd6831 (2016); wd7972 (2019); wd6562 (2016) This idea of paintings as ledgers or accretions of activity is hyper-concentrated in the wd series ("warehouse drawings"). Landis produced 10,000 wd pieces in the nearly thirty years between October 1996 and March 2025. Nearly all began as a folded piece of paper that Landis would carry with him throughout the day, often marked with notes, reminders, shopping lists. "Later in the studio, I chronologically staple them to boards, usually working on 20 at a time, drawing and painting on them, often in multiple layers over many days, weeks and sometimes months in response to whatever is happening in my world at each session." Like a recording of an improvised performance, the wd paintings are the record of happenings that can't ever be restaged, a ledger of events that could never be repeated exactly so. Their accumulation of texture, their creases and sometimes ragged edges, are evidence of their travel through the real world, are the grounding reminders that, however abstract the visuals, they are the products of a creative drive that is selfsame with Landis, moving through life. Though Landis has retired the wd series, hints of their methodology have emerged in a new FP series created on small pieces of folded hand-made paper. Left to Right: FP26.78 (2026); FP26.103 (2026); FP26.174 (2026) Paintings from the wd series often made their way back to music, and the influence began running in the opposite direction. Several have been used as album art, and over the years musicians would ask Landis if they could use a painting as inspiration for music. Most notably, Loren Connors and Suzanne Langille took a number of wd pieces and projected them in the studio while recording, which was subsequently released as I Wish I Didn't Dream . During the pandemic, Landis began a series of smaller, heavily contingent paintings called "Notes." Each month, he starts dozens, which he lays around the house or beneath paintings in the studio, allowing them to gather stains and marks of daily life. "Notes" can be shuffled and combined into larger pieces called "Compositions," forming the basis of graphic scores. In 2024, the Cannery in Penobscot, Maine staged a series of concerts in which "Compositions" were performed by musicians like E. Jason Gibbs, Phillip Greenlief, Leslie Ross, Steve Norton, Laura Cromwell, and others. Top, Left to Right: Note 138 (2020); Note 126 (2020); Note 154 (2020); Note 1131 (2026) Bottom, Left to Right: Note 964 (2025); Note 1121 (2026); Note 1 (2020); Note 702 (2023) Accepting that there's something more than brute, unskilled doing behind such vast and varied artistic output, the "overweening" approach—a propensity I admit I must actively temper—starts from trying to articulate the interesting whatness of all those coalesced particularities . But it can be quick to flight and risks overstating its case. In seeking some ultimate source for often dumbfounding glimpses into a pure creative stream, it also risks leaving the artist behind entirely. Firebrand critic Robert Hughes famously had little patience for this. He once wrote that all of the "verbose obeisances to the Ineffable" in discussions of Mark Rothko's work tended "to be coercive, because of a deep uncertainty about the nature of his art." (I'm not sure what Hughes would make of something like Paint & Drums, though I can imagine him satisfied, standing before the large paintings at the end of the show, still gleaming and dripping.) Hughes's warning is not unfounded, but it's also dismissive of the role uncertainty and small-i ineffability play in the experience of art like Landis's (or Rothko's, for that matter). We find the ineffable creeping up not because this sort of art is a direct mainline to the transcendent Godhead or a manifestation of universal Truth, but because it carries the possibility of ringing within us some deeply sympathetic tone, a personal and close-feeling resonance that never quite carries through into words. This isn't absolute or guaranteed. In truth, it is fleeting and infrequent. But we each know our own private tone and we hope in our encounters to feel that vibration. Returning to Cavell, in "Music Discomposed" he says these kinds of art are " known by feeling , or in feeling," and this underlies our anxiety and difficulty in communicating this knowledge: "I want to tell you something I've seen, or heard, or realized, or come to understand, for the reasons for which such things are communicated (because it is news, about a world we share, or could). Only I find that I can't tell you; and that makes it all the more urgent to tell you. I want to tell you because the knowledge, unshared, is a burden . . . It matters, there is a burden, because unless I can tell you what I know, there is a suggestion (and to myself as well) that I do not know." This uncertainty is not a defect. It is an essential component of the improvised musical set, and of Landis's practice as he steps into his studio each day and faces dozens of paintings in various stages. And, Hughes's self-certainty aside, I think it is also the essential, brightly dark core of our aesthetic experience of these works. It's the same doubt the skeptic amplifies until it distorts into nothingness, easy to dismiss. Uncertainty—not-quite-knowing—is the grip that pulls the artist into the stream, and it's also the grip that gets us by the collar and stops us, to look or to listen. Picking up a paint brush or a saxophone are also attempts to convey news about a world we share, or could. Left: 15.14 (2015); Right: 20.03 (2020) "Somehow Precise, Intense, and Vague All at Once" The heading is Michael Gallope's description of what he calls music's "affective inconsistency," but it also beautifully captures Landis's paintings and the particular energy of his live collaboration with Sarin. One of the more charming aspects of Landis's and Sarin's partnership is that they still aren't quite sure of it. Each time, they gently ease into a start and there's always some hesitation about whether they've finished. This thread of uncertainty runs through the whole performance, is what fuels the excitement, but it also feels more palpable than during a musical improvisation. Left: M P Landis and Michael Sarin, May 15, 2024 at the Apohadion Theater, Portland, ME Top Right: P+D 04 01 03 (2026); Bottom Right: P+D 03 02 02 (2026) In the audience, witnessing the real-time change in the paintings draws out tensions between arising aesthetic judgments and a curiosity about what continuing will yield. As elements emerge in the paintings, there are times when things "feel" finished, or where particular sections or forms satisfy some personal preference. I find myself becoming protective, secretly wishing that further actions will spare a notable swirl of black or a blaze of orange that still burns though layer after layer. I wasn't alone. At several of the performances, others talked about fearing a painting was "ruined" at points during the show, feeling satisfied with a certain stage of the process and forgetting that the process must continue, that the painting in the moment they esteemed it also arose by that process. After the April 2026 performance, one enthusiastic young audience member bantered with Landis about the range of emotions he felt during the show: "At one point, I actually felt angry with you, man! I thought you fucked it up!" Imagining how you think someone should be behaving toward certain sounds or stimuli also leads to subverted expectations. I wonder if the way Landis is moving should be more . . . what? Theatrical? Synchronized? Wouldn't that be inauthentic? How do I suppose live painting and drumming should look, and where'd those ideas even come from? It feels like the risks of improvising are magnified. And are they greater for M P? Notes melt away, but marks on canvas remain. Left: P+D 01 02 04 (2024); Center: P+D 01 01 03 (2024); Right: P+D 02 02 08 (2024) It's all quite different from watching two musicians improvising. At times they seem at odds, or moving just past one another. Sarin whips himself into a storm, a deluge of creative energy that—in my mind—is an arc of electricity shooting across the stage to directly animate M P's limbs. But Landis is opening a paint bottle or looking for a brush. All that, just dissipated! But has it? I presume bolts of lightning, but am likely missing the charged potential in the air. In some ways, it becomes easier to sense these shifting emotions when there's a visual element, a continuing remnant. In music alone, things often move so quickly that only the most egregious "missteps" or a complete failure to gel create notable feelings of resistance in the witness. Here, things move as fast, but your eyes are drawn to the canvas, which holds on to the movement of the performance like streaks of light in a long exposure. Through all these contours, there's an unmistakable resonance between what Landis and Sarin are doing, if not an equivalence. I feel an immense mental force that wants to draw their activities into a neat consonance, but it's like pushing repelling magnets together. As Landis has always maintained, the painting doesn't "represent" the sounds any more than the reverse. Instead, there's a joyous, if ambiguous, exchange of energy. You can see that it's mutually reinforcing. Sarin is palpably exhilarated. The propulsion of his drumming spurs Landis into action, and the emerging images become mutable graphic scores, giant ever-changing "notes" urging Sarin further. The exact how just evades a tight grasp. Together or separately, the painting and drumming are abstract art that many would accuse of being untethered. But there's something stubbornly literal in their doing. The paintings are just that: caked and layered paint, ink, and pastel, thick and viscous or water-thinned and dripping. The drums: driving, rhythmic, sometimes crashing, deafening, sometimes the faintest texture of hand's skin on drumskin. It is all, plainly, what it is, a frustrating tautology because there is yet, as Sarin said at the end of the most recent performance, an alchemy. "Whole" and "Divided" Painting from Paint & Drums 4, May 9, 2026 at the Loove Annex, Brooklyn, NY Fever Bed To quote another M-P, Maurice Merleau-Ponty wrote in "Cézanne's Doubt" that "before expression, there is nothing but a vague fever, and only the work itself, completed and understood, will prove that there was something rather than nothing to be found there." I'd gently propose shifting the sense of the word "work": M-P wrote l'œuvre , a finished piece of art, an "artifact" of the creative act. I'd like to read it as the doing, le faire, le travail —the undertaking of creating. I often sense that vague fever while listening to improvised music, like the back of my hand against a warm forehead, and admittedly less often when facing a painting. I vicariously feel it in the dim light, watching Landis and Sarin on stage. Still, I sense in myself an inhibiting self-consciousness, like I'd never be able to start, even as I also discover expectations and opinions welling up and fading away as the performance plays out. Once in motion, there's an odd sort of courage in continuing to mark the canvas, to pound the drum, but I wonder if the central task of the improvising artist is to continually overcome that uneasy inertia and just begin . An unstopping at imagination's edge that risks mistake and awkwardness and dissatisfaction to possibly reach something that at best can only be hazily made out, and not at all while sitting in caution and doubt. Unsure if you can know you've reached it. Something about the feeling of reaching. items._cn_summary: 这篇文章围绕画家M P Landis的专辑及与鼓手Michael Sarin的'Paint & Drums'即兴合作展开。文中详细描述了2024至2026年间在缅因州波特兰Apohadion剧院的现场创作场景：画板悬挂在鼓组旁，铺满纸张并以白色胶带划分网格，颜料瓶与罐盖散落其间。Landis将抽象表现主义的视觉语汇与自由即兴音乐的精神相融合，通过音乐触发身体动作，在画布上完成从儿童般稚拙到充满目的性的笔触。文章引用了他与作家Fred Schmalz的对话，以及Mike Heffley在《Northern Sun, Southern Moon》中的论述，阐明音乐如何成为画家进入创作状态的媒介。Landis为多张专辑绘制封面，包括Flow Trio、[ism]和Sabir Mateen的作品，其画作常以所聆听的音乐命名，如致敬Joe Maneri的《PIANO SKY》及致敬Derek Bailey的lp13.06。文章呈现了视觉艺术与即兴音乐之间深层的相互渗透关系。

items.body: Canadian netlabel Panospria released “I-II-III”, the debut album under the Silver Shadow name, on 15 July 2026. It runs to 26 tracks across three volumes gathered into a single digital set, sold in MP3 and FLAC from 15 Canadian dollars, and it moves between IDM, ambient, drone and minimal techno. The release page presents the album as three distinct volumes compiled into one, and as the latest work of a long-standing name on the label. It never prints that name: “Having recently relocated to France from Canada, keen listeners will surely deduce the identity of this mainstay on our label. New country, new alias, new directions in music.” The label’s own announcement is less coy than the release page. It presents Silver Shadow as the new alias of the artist formerly recording as Silent Q and Gyges. Both of those names belong to Paul Keeley, a Montreal electronic producer whose Gyges album “Composite Massive” was Panospria’s second release in 2004 and who has issued deep and progressive house under his own name through Thinner, Epsilonlab and Anjunadeep. The Silver Shadow Bandcamp page gives the artist’s location as Paris. What is on the Silver Shadow album ‘I-II-III’ The three volumes are not new to the same degree. Volume I is the eight-track album “I”, put on Bandcamp on 26 July 2022, and volume II is the ten-track “II” from 22 November 2024; the remaining eight tracks, from “Delores” to “Matte”, appear here for the first time. II by Silver Shadow Track titles run as compressed fragments throughout: “Aieesqvb96”, “nFU-VHToT”, “HshShsHs”, “HpnoTod”, “Grgwld”, “Dickenszs”. In order the album reads Aieesqvb96, Fulter, Plyurs, nFU-VHToT, Crunge, Duke, Spong, Purf, Ghosnen, AmbWks, Mmoonn, TheLab, Pull, HshShsHs, HpnoTod, Unstld, Grgwld, Roogah, Delores, KiBC8, NewWav, Sheets, Dickenszs, Krud, Thumb and Matte. About Silver Shadow and Panospria Silver Shadow first appeared on Bandcamp on 3 April 2020 with the five-track “A”, followed by “I” in 2022 and “II” in 2024, so the Panospria set is a label debut rather than a first release under the alias. Panospria itself grew out of the Canadian prairies around the turn of the millennium and put out its first offering, the “Alphaform” compilation, in 2002 with Dublin’s Psychonavigation. The label was properly established in Montreal that same year and was among the earliest to treat the MP3 as a release format in its own right. It moved with its operators, running from Montreal until 2008, then Vancouver, then Saskatoon from 2022. Alongside the catalogue it ran two concert series: Textures in Montreal and Quiet City in Vancouver, the latter reaching 70 editions over a decade. In 2007 the Panospria catalogue was folded into the Montreal netlabel No Type, which has been active since 1998 and also runs Annexe, BricoLodge, Nishi and Sine Fiction; Panospria has operated as a No Type sublabel since. Paul Keeley’s connection to the label goes back almost to the start. The Gyges record “Composite Massive” carried the second catalogue number in 2004, and he has since appeared on Panospria releases by Heart & Soul, Shoebomber, Arnau Sala and N4K3D D1G1TS. “I-II-III” is the first Silver Shadow release Panospria has issued, and by the label’s account the first since the move from Canada to France.

items.body: Hocico needs no introduction to any fan of Dark-Electro. The Mexican duo has been active continuously since 1993, delivering countless hits and brilliant albums. This new album took a little longer to arrive—around four years—and is available with an extra disc and/or vinyl featuring six additional tracks, including three remixes, one of them by Funker Vogt. With “Unseen Horror Scenes”, Hocico takes aim at various aspects of our contemporary world. Our environment has been in decline for some time, providing a potent source of inspiration for the duo. Musically, the album contains classic, instantly recognizable Hocico tracks infused with a heavy dose of power and aggression. They remain relentless in this regard, yet highly effective in their compositions and rage-filled vocals. However, the album also seeks to introduce some innovation. We encounter various experiments, ranging from pure Electro-Punk and a breakbeat-driven track to Cinematic instrumentals and even a song featuring a touch of Rap. Notably, the main album contains only one Spanish-language track, which is a departure from their usual approach. Hocico has been trying to introduce some evolution into their work over the years, an effort I certainly applaud. Unfortunately, they do not quite succeed on this record. Despite a few strong tracks, I am left feeling somewhat unsatisfied. “Unseen Horror Scenes” has merit on many levels, but it is certainly not the album I would choose to introduce Hocico to someone who has just discovered the Dark-Electro scene. Not every album can be the best. (Rating:7). Listen to “The Screen”: The Screen by Hocico About Hocico Hocico is the Mexican electro-industrial duo of cousins Erik Garcia (Erk Aicrag, vocals and lyrics) and Oscar Mayorga (Racso Agroyam, synthesizers and programming). The pair formed the project in Mexico City in 1993, taking their stage names as reversals of their given names, and played their first concert on 18 February 1994. Early cassette releases such as “Autoagresión Persistente” and “Misuse, Abuse And Accident” in 1994 and “Triste Desprecio” in 1996 were self-released. The studio albums that followed include “Odio Bajo El Alma” in 1997, “El Día De La Ira” in 1998, “Sangre Hirviente” in 1999, “Signos De Aberracion” in 2002, “Wrack And Ruin” in 2004, “Memorias Atrás” in 2008, “Tiempos De Furia” in 2010, “El Último Minuto (Antes De Que Tu Mundo Caiga)” in 2012, “Ofensor” in 2015, “The Spell Of The Spider” in 2017, “Artificial Extinction” in 2019 and “HyperViolent” in 2022. The duo records for Out Of Line. Recent releases on the label include the four-track “The Screen” EP in March 2025 and the collaboration with Prayers on “Hey Tú” in November 2025, expanded into a four-track EP in December 2025. “Unseen Horror Scenes” arrives four years after “HyperViolent” and was announced by Side-Line in May 2026.
items._cn_summary: 墨西哥双人组Hocico暌违四年带来新作《Unseen Horror Scenes》，延续其标志性的力量感与侵略性，合成器编排密集且愤怒的演唱贯穿始终。专辑主题聚焦当代世界的环境恶化与社会批判，融入多种实验元素：纯电子朋克段落、碎拍驱动曲目、电影化器乐作品，以及一首带有说唱色彩的歌曲，仅一首西班牙语曲目成为对其惯常路线的偏离。乐评肯定乐队追求演变的意图，但认为执行不够理想，整体虽有亮点却未能成为向新听众推介Hocico的首选作品。制作由独立厂牌Out of Line发行，包含六首额外曲目的加量版本。

items.body: The clunk with which Michael Cutting’s “STILLS” begins is an instantly recognisable sound for most people who are either above a certain age, or enjoying playing with audiovisual equipment older than they are: it’s the sound of a finger-sized metal or plastic button being pressed and mechanically engaging some kind of playback process. In this case, judging by album images and also by how it sounds, the button likely belongs to a modified cassette player, projector, or some other tape- or film-playing device with spinning wheels and other moving parts. Cutting is one half of Kinder Meccano (the other half being Vitalija Glovackyte), and the interest in DIY, modified, and adapted electronics spills over from that project into his solo work. “STILLS” is more focused, however, involving mostly manipulations of tape playback. That clunk is followed by quiet; then gentle, swirling tones, ringing in timbre, looping, rhythmically tumbling round and over one another. It’s a concoction at once strange and familiar, soothing and anxious at the same time. The next piece’s uptempo, almost jazzy syncopated chords roll to halt, then start up again, joined by rough, sharp-edged tones. The pace then relents for a while, with gently screeching pitches over ambiguous warm chords, before a bass drop leads to quivering guitar rhythms. That slight jazzy tinge returns later on in the album, this time in hushed long notes from what sound like muted trumpets, quiet chimes with building hum, beep, and crackle. Cutting’s use of melody — plaintive, jaunty, occasionally drifting off-key — perfectly suits the nature of his tape-based ‘instruments’, with their inherent flaws, uncertainties, and means of making sound. It is almost as if he seeks to give voice to the personalities of devices such as old tape decks and reel projectors, or at least project a certain character onto them. Take the rapid flurries of cheerful melody in the piece ‘SLATE’, for example, which eventually fade, stumble, and finally give way to slow, slightly sad chords: with a bit of imagination, one hears the mood swings of a playful mechanical child. “STILLS” is full of such attractive contrasts of melody, harmony, and rhythm, made all the more compelling by the ways in which they incorporate the material nature of the machines and processes that produce them. The album ends, back where it began, with the clunk of a button. items._cn_summary: 这张专辑围绕改装卡带播放器、放映器等老旧机械设备展开声音探索。专辑以一声按钮按下的机械撞击声开篇，贯穿始终，形成了首尾呼应的结构框架。Michael Cutting利用磁带播放的物理特性——转速、循环、失真——作为作曲素材，生成流动、旋转的音色。作品中融合了缓慢起伏的和弦、尖锐的边缘音、爵士色彩的和声以及类似柔和铜管的低音线条，让机械设备仿佛拥有了自己的情绪与性格。旋律时而哀伤、时而跳跃、偶有跑调，恰好契合了这些介质固有的不稳定性与不确定性。这种创作思路将机器的物质属性纳入作曲逻辑，使声音缺陷本身成为表达的一部分。专辑收录于独立小型厂牌，延续了作者与Vitalija Glovackyte合作的Kinder Meccano项目中DIY电子改装的精神。

items.body: A confession to begin: I�ve been a fan of Alison Cotton�s music for quite a while, so the announcement of a new album definitely brought me a frisson of delight. The Gods Laugh certainly doesn�t disappoint, with the same deliciously amorphous feel that�s defined her other work, drawing on folk, the avant-garde, as well as a sense of religiosity to make the music here, possibly best exemplified in �I Am!�, where she set a poem by John Clare, England�s great nature poet, to a transcendent melody over the constant underpinning of a lulling drone. While the playing revolves around her usual arsenal of viola, harmonium, hammered dulcimer, and piano, along with some percussion, on this album she also adds some drums, bass and synthesizer. The music is often improvised and captured in a single take, with an almost mystical, hushed sensibility that seems to reach through time, as with �I Still Know You are Calling My Name,� where the tune could have been plucked from an old folk song. Sprigs of Heather by Alison Cotton The centerpiece, however, is �Sprigs of Heather,� with an opening that recalls medieval sacred music that becomes a simple, slowly cascading, piano-led melody. It�s far from the longest track on the album, but a little pearl of perfection that carries the listener away. Sprigs of Heather by Alison Cotton The Gods Laugh is a memorial of sorts to Cotton�s father, who died in late 2024. There�s a sense of loss reaching across these tracks, most specifically present on �The Final Harvest,� a solemn piece about her father�s last visit to the allotment he loved so much. It�s suffused with tenderness that extends beyond words. Light and darkness bleed into each other across the music, and moods shift. It�s music that happily stands beyond category, with hints of so many things, but ultimately standing as Alison Cotton music, which might well be all the definition it needs. It will challenge you but also satisfy and move you. What more can you wish from music? Find the artist online. More to hear: United States of Alchemy - Songs of Compassion (Review) Dani Jan� - Vida (Review)

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑延续了Alison Cotton一贯的模糊风格边界，融合民谣、前卫音乐与中世纪宗教音乐的气质。乐器编制以中提琴、簧风琴、击弦古钢琴和钢琴为主，加入鼓、贝斯和合成器扩展音色层次。大量作品采用即兴方式一次录制完成，营造出穿越时空的神秘而低语的氛围。中段'Sprigs of Heather'以中世纪圣咏风格开篇，随后转为钢琴主导的缓慢级进旋律，成为全作核心。整张专辑也是Cotton对2024年末去世父亲的纪念，'The Final Harvest'以其父亲最后一次造访心爱的菜园为主题，弥漫着难以言喻的温柔。光与暗在不同曲目间渗透流转，情绪持续变化，最终呈现为一种难以归类的、属于Cotton自身的音乐语言。

items.body: Those of us who have been digging into Analog Africa�s increasingly formidable releases over the last two decades are well aware of the massive amount of raw, vodun-based Sato and Sakpata-derived funk the label has issued by Benin�s most prolific 1970s-era band, the Orchestre Poly-Ritmo. AA has dropped no fewer than 3 compilations of their heaviest material, as well as a reissue of the band�s first LP, in an effort to give them the international status they deserve. That being said, what might be different about this collection of their music? And who is Antoine Dougb�? Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa As it turns out, Dougb� was a song-conjurer whose mode of musical transfer was slapping his legs in a rhythm known as Cavacha, a groove created by drummer Belobi Meridjo, who was inspired by a train cadence that he worked into a pattern that ultimately spread like a 21st century California wildfire throughout Congolese pop music in the mid-1970s. Dougb�, known as the �Devil�s Prime Minister,� was also a practitioner of vodun who inspired fear in any musician he felt was unsuited to play his music, which is how he landed on working exclusively Poly-Ritmo, as he felt they could nail what he wanted in ways other bands couldn�t. His recording career was brief - 3 albums and a few singles - but as this collection shows, it was potent. Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa Because of the era from which this music dates, it�s not surprising that the recording and instrument tones have changed - the guitars have a plastic sheen and synthesizers appear- even if the music remains rooted in the 1970s. Perhaps the influence of the Cuban son is more apparent here than on other Poly-Ritmo collections, especially in the collection�s initial offerings. And yes, Congolese rumba, then shaking all of sub-Saharan Africa to its knees, is present too. �Ma Won Min Towe Leo� is one example. Opening with a bed of synthesizers, the shimmering guitars, tinny, seemingly squeezed dry by the 80s themselves, lock in over relentless high-hat-focused grooves. The guitars finally start firing in different directions midway through, before that synth weaves back in, forming a bed underneath it all. Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa �We Tayi Sin Assi Tche� is much more overtly Cuban. With its insistent cowbell, classic, nasal vocal call and response, and tight, repeated guitar figures, its debt to mid-twentieth century Afro-Cuban sons is transparent. Another track, �Djomido Ma Dougbe Tche� rides a groove reminiscent of 70�s-era Franco classic �Liberte.� The pulse is relentless, and the guitar solo repeats a tight repetition of a few notes, driving listeners to ecstasy all the while. However, none of this music is a mere copy of its influences; rather, like so much potent pop coming from the continent at the time, it is a swirl of major influences rendered by local rhythms and vocal phrasing to give it specific identity, in this case, to Benin. Dougb�s musical role on this collection is a bit murky. One of his three albums has a photo of him, fully mic�d behind a collection of hand drums, so perhaps he served as a percussionist/vocalist; this release never explains. He wasn�t a songwriter in the traditional sense. It seems he was more of an instigator and arranger, but his thumbprint was apparently heavy enough to warrant his name on the records he was involved with. Whatever the case, in his brief run as a recording artist, he and Poly-Ritmo produced a handful of driving, Cavacha-inspired grooves that can still wear holes in club floors. Further reading: Petrona Mart�nez - Ancestras (Review) Gnonnas Pedro & His Dadjes - Roi De L'Agbadja Moderne 1974-1983 (Review)

items._cn_summary: 这张合辑聚焦贝宁传奇乐队Orchestre Poly-Rythmo与歌手Antoine Dougbé在1977至1982年间的合作作品。Dougbé以拍腿节奏Cavacha著称，该节奏源自鼓手Belobi Meridjo对火车节奏的提炼，后风靡刚果流行乐界。音乐根植于伏都教传统，吉他音色带有明显的塑料质感与八十年代合成器底色，古巴颂乐与刚果伦巴的影响在多首作品中清晰可辨。编曲上，合成器铺垫与细薄吉他交织在高帽主导的律动之上，器乐对话层次丰富。作为Analog Africa厂牌对这支西非乐队的又一次系统性梳理，合辑展现了被低估的贝宁音乐传统如何与泛非及加勒比风格交汇，形成兼具仪式感与舞池能量的声音。

items.body: Tako Toki are like desert island musicians who, castaway without their instruments, were forced to construct their own. Lucky for us, they are as skilled in making instruments as they are in creating original songs with which to show off their handicrafts. Un Dimanche � Monaco is the band�s follow-up to their well-received debut, Hirsute Farfelus , with a similar mash of musical styles. Before discussing the music, we need to talk about their instrument closet. They really have built everything they play out of bric-a-brac, odds and ends, and rubbish. I�m not sure from listening which is which, but they call their instruments, in an incomplete list, tassofons, tilofons, and tubofones, clarinuts, didjerimou, and klarbass, and my favorite, kitchenofon. (I will refer to what I hear by the names of store-bought instruments that they sound like.) The most surprising thing for me was how accurate the instruments were to pitch and how good they sounded under the harsh scrutiny of modern recording microphones that have documented a rich, high-quality sound. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki They have also very effectively matched their choice of instruments with the style of music that inspires their compositions. Right off the top, �Yinitza� features a laughing clarinet singing a klezmer tune accompanied by bassoon for the bass, frantic two-time percussion, and the exuberant human yelps found on many klezmer recordings. As on this track, many tunes feature improvisations that show an impressive degree of musicianship. On the cumbia-inspired �Le Cuenta,� the characteristic flute carries the tune, augmented by a Spanish singing chorus, and remarkably rich-sounding Latin percussion. The title track surrounds us with afrobeat woodblocks, shakers, and rattles scattered around the mix. The melody is played on a marimba ornamented with bells and cymbals. Again, the lead player improvises over the tune and often against the beat with jazzy chops. The flute returns on the samba-inspired �Ambiguidade,� and on �Aksum� it traces a trance-like Middle Eastern tune reminiscent of a 60s TV spy-show theme. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki Full of fun and one of a kind, Un Dimanche � Monaco celebrates our universal love of rhythmic, melodic, and harmonic sounds and the varied, wonderful ways cultures have organized that love in what we call music. At the same time, playing on literal pieces of junk, Tako Tiko reminds us, as we contemplate many mall music shops filled with gleaming wood and brass instruments and countless unused guitars lying in closets, that musicians will always find a way to make music. Find the artist online. Further reading: Tako Toki - Hirsute Farfelus (Review) Terje Isungset - Glacial Poetry (Review)

items._cn_summary: Tako Toki的专辑《Un Dimanche à Monaco》展现了用废旧材料自制乐器的独特创作方式，乐器包括tassofons、kitchenofon等自造装置，在现代录音技术下依然音准精确、音色饱满。乐队将克莱兹默、昆比亚、桑巴、阿弗罗贝特、中东旋律等多种世界音乐风格融合，每首曲目对应不同的文化主题。《Yinitza》以单簧管模仿克莱兹默哭腔伴以巴松与打击乐；《Le Cuenta》呈现拉丁打击乐与西班牙合唱；同名曲运用阿弗罗贝特木鱼与马林巴；中东旋律曲目则有60年代间谍剧般的恍惚感。专辑传递了一种普世理念：音乐的本质在于节奏、旋律与和声的文化组织方式，而非乐器的物质载体。

items.body: After the extra-terrestial explorations of Eventyrferd , the previous album from Norway's Camilla Hole Trio, in which sci-fi synth sounds were married with traditional material, their latest release Langs is rather more earthbound. But the quest to look beyond their own country's folk music continues. Camilla Hole's main instrument being the soprano sax, the influence of jazz is unsurprising and this is evident in the opening track �Springleik,� signifying a tune used to accompany the springleik dance from the west of Norway. Initially Hole takes the melody with Egil Kalman and Knut Kvifte Nesheim providing rhythmic support on double bass and drums respectively, with the overdubbing of Kalman's modular synth and Nesheim's vibraphone adding colour. But characteristically for this trio, in which assigned roles are never clearly defined or adhered to, things soon start to move around, with Kalman taking up the melody on his bass, playing the melody in unison with Hole, while Nesheim opens things out further rhythmically. As the whole piece takes on a much more improvisatory feel, Hole plays the melody one more time as things draw to a close. Langs by Camilla Hole Trio
items.label: Taragot
items._cn_summary: 挪威Camilla Hole Trio的新专辑《Langs》延续了上一张《Eventyrferd》中对外星声音的探索，但更回归本土。乐队以高音萨克斯为主奏乐器，融合挪威西部传统民间旋律与爵士即兴，同时引入模块合成器和颤音琴作为色彩层。乐评重点分析开场曲Springleik的处理方式：起初由萨克斯主奏旋律，低音提琴和鼓提供节奏支撑，随后合成器与颤音琴的叠加逐渐打破固定的角色分配，旋律与节奏在成员之间流动转换，最终萨克斯再次回归旋律收束全曲。这种模糊乐器职能、鼓励即兴交互的做法，体现了乐队在传统与现代、爵士与民俗之间的跨界探索。

items._cn_summary: 这是Metapsychosis Continuum系列的第二部作品，由Philippe Petit创作的电声作品Slea Head，创作周期跨越2023至2025年。作品从一首短诗出发，将诗歌中的意象转化为质感、音高、运动与沉浸式的声场结构，体现出从文本到声音的转译过程。Petit本人附有一段关于当代电声音乐作为开放、持续演变的实践的简短陈述。该作品延续了系列对实验性声音探索的关注，融合诗歌、电声作曲与沉浸式聆听体验，属于小众实验音乐范畴。由于原文为新闻类简讯而非完整乐评，信息量有限，难以深入评估其实际音响细节与艺术成就，但就其创作理念与方法论而言，与当代实验音乐的前沿探索方向一致。

items.body: Review by BrufordFreak — Sticking together for one more album, Roger Sutton's Riff Raff pull off another very cool Jazz Rock album--something edging its way into the Canterbury conversation. Perhaps working in Kent (where Canterbury lies) with producer Ken Burgess (who would go on to work with Tommy Eyre's next band, Zzebra) had something to do with that.1. "Original Man" (7:40) this Peter Kirtley composition opens with a one minute whole band intro that borders on sounding like something from one of their Canterbury contemporaries, but then in the second minute things settle down into a very cool almost downtempo ambient electric lounge music over which Peter sings in a bit of a Dylanesque style. Peter's lead guitar play in the middle portends the coming of Stevie Ray Vaughan as well as paying a bit of an homage to his contemporary, Eric Clapton. What a great, powerful song to open an album with! Signs of good things to come! (14.375/15)2. "Havakak" (6:06) another really cool Jazz-Rock Fusion song that sounds like something National Health or The Soft Machine would have done. There is just such a great warmth to the feel of this palette and the soundscape it creates: no matter if the band is ripping through it (first motif), slowing things down (second motif), blues-rocking it (third motif), or vamping for Peter Kirtley's extended solo (fourth motif), the sound just wraps around you and makes you feel a part of it. And to think it was a composition that Peter brought from working with keyboard master Kenny Craddock and bassist Colin Gibson during their Mark-Almond days! (9.75/10)3. "Goddamm the Man" (6:09) a Roger Sutton original places us in a juke joint in the Louisiana/Mississippi swamp as raw steel-string acoustic guitars pick away Jack Johnson style from both the left and right while Roger's funky bass and Aureo's drums and congas and Tommy Eyre's stanky electric piano and organ add and increase the funky stink (everybody seems to have taken on at least two tracks). I didn't think I was going to like this once it opened (especially with Roger's Swamp-style American White Blues vocals) but once it got going, once the background vocals and horn section's accents were added, the funk just took over: I'm a fan! (9.25/10)4. "In the Deep" (3:59) Oh, my gosh! Is Robert Wyatt in the house? Peter Kirtley's second offering to the album finds us deep in the forlorn ballad forms that reluctantly came out of the Canterbury Scene. There is so much funky R&B in this--and it feels so solid and natural! Every nuance and subtlety injected, added, and feels so perfect, so genius, so easy! Shades of two of the best to ever do this style: Paddy McAloon (Prefab Sprout) and Roddy Frame (Aztec Camera) as well as the contemporary master extemporaneosifier, Richard Sinclair. Awesome and alarmingly good! (9.75/10)5. "The Waster" (5:09) feels a bit like a continuation or variation on a palette, pace, and style used in all of the previous songs (the sound French downtempo band AIR mastered for their massive hit, >). Roger Sutton's second composition finds him drifting more into the singing style of Eric Burdon (think "Drink This Wine"; even the lyrical format is very much like that iconic song). I love the laid-back vibe of the musicians' spacious note and chord play, a late night application of funk. Horn accents, smooth Fender Rhodes, congas and drums, background vocals, bluesy rhythm guitar, lead sax in the instrumental section, nice, easy-going two-chord construct (think Traffic's "Feelin' Alright"). It's nice, it's fun, it's warm, it's equally well performed as the album's previous material, just a little more tranquilizing. (8.875/10)6. "Tom's Song" (4:22) the title, of course, referring to keyboardist Tommy Eyre, who is the composer of this song. Though it starts out having a little trouble defining itself and its melodies for the first minute, it eventually metes out some quite lovely music: the piano playing and synth strings support quite lush and romantic. Roger's bass and Aureo's congas are muted into the background leaving the synth strings, piano, voice, and Steve Gregory's weirdly-effected flutes in the foreground. Tom's vocal is rather gentle, doubled up, I think. It's obviously a sad love song about regret. I like it's edgy classical and jazz influences as well as Tom's genuine emotion. (9/10)7. "Speed" (9:16) another great construct from multiple influences: the funky blues, American Southern Rock, Traffic, The Allman Brothers, and a little Van Morrison and The Doors in the mix. Another Roger Sutton original, I consider this to be not a particularly great or memorable "epic" but definitely another serious and high quality rendering. (17.625/20)Total Time 42:41It feels weird to be categorizing music coming from Great Britain with labels like "Southern Rock," "Swamp Rock" or "American Southern Rock" but they would not be the only British artists attracted to those types of American sounds. (Think of Alan Parker's film The Commitments and its characters' connection to the Memphis Horns and the music of Wilson Pickett.) Almost every British artist who was coming of age in the early 1960s would cite American Blues, Soul, R&B, and even Jazz as essential foundations and inspirations for their music. Roger Sutton, Peter Kirtley, Tommy Eyre, and Bud Beadle would be no different. I do, however, give the band credit for hearing and emulating a bit of their own countrymates of the Canterbury Style.A/five stars; an eclectic and full-blown masterpiece of sophisticated and highly-nuanced original music by some sadly-under-appreciated musicians (and band). HIGHLY recommended to any professed and self-respecting music lover.
items._cn_summary: 这是RIFF RAFF乐队1974年专辑《Original Man》的乐评，专辑延续了Canterbury场景的爵士摇滚融合路线。开场曲长达七分半，包含乐队齐奏引子后转入氛围化电爵士段落，Peter Kirtley的吉他演奏被比作Stevie Ray Vaughan与Clapton的混合体。第二首由Kirtley与Mark-Almond时期合作者共同创作的曲目，展现了柔软的音色质感，在四种动机间灵活切换。第三首Roger Sutton的原创作品以路易斯安那沼泽蓝调开场，加入放克节奏后逐渐转变为更具感染力的律动。第四首慢板抒情曲被拿来与Robert Wyatt、Prefab Sprout、Aztec Camera以及Richard Sinclair等风格相比较，融合R&B与Canterbury式的忧郁气息。整体专辑虽带有Canterbury标签，但融合了蓝调、放克与美式民谣元素，呈现出温暖而多彩的爵士摇滚图景。

items.body: The Greek duo—comprising George Katsanos and Irini Tiniakou—formed their musical alter ego, Incirrina, in Athens in 2017. This year, they released their third full-length album, “Trace”, via the German label Cold Transmission Music. Over the years, their sound and influences have steadily evolved from Dark-Wave towards a style leaning more towards Minimal/Electro-Wave, featuring Irini’s icy vocals. The result is a distinctive soundscape that evokes a sense of 1980s nostalgia through its cold analogue tones. I caught up with the duo for an entertaining and informative chat, and they left a lasting impression on me—not only as passionate artists, but also as incredibly kind and appreciative people. (Courtesy by Inferno Sound Diaries) Q: “Trace” is already your third full-length album. Looking back on everything you’ve achieved so far, how do you view your journey as a band? And how would you describe and introduce this new record to people who may not have heard it yet? George: Indeed, after the releases of the albums “8.15” (2019) and “Lip Led Scream” (2022), we are happy to have our third LP “Trace” out by the label Cold Transmission, released 29.5.2026. We consider the band as a space for exploration, experimentation, personal expression, also as an inner journey and diving into our souls. Incirrina has brought us the joy of sharing our music with people across multiple countries. Until now we have toured in 12 European countries and played in many gigs and Festivals, which led to beautiful and completely new experiences. Irini: In this album, we experimented with instrumentation, rhythm and vocal approach. We used a combination of analogue synthesizers, drum machines, octapad, electric bass guitar, electric piano and acoustic instruments such as kantele, waterphone, melodica. “Trace” includes 11 songs written between 2023-2025 in a 24-channel console, that belong in the genres of Dark-Electronic, Synth-Wave and Cold-Wave. The Minimal-Synth and Post-Punk roots of our previous albums are still obvious, yet the new songs are enriched with dynamism, depth, and rhythmic diversity and we also explored new ways of delivering the vocals for this album. Also we would like to note that this album is the result of the collaboration of many people who put their heart and talent into it, and we are grateful to them -these people are Dimitris Dimitriadis (mixing), Anestis Psaradakos (mastering), uBuDancer (ArtWork-AnalogueCollage), Nestor Theophilopoulos (photography), Maria Deligiorgi/Infrared Media (Layout) and Suzy Hermann and Andreas Hermann of Cold Transmission. Q: If I’m not mistaken, you’ve been active for almost ten years now. How did Incirrina come into being, and how have both your collaboration and the band itself evolved over the years? George: Our common journey as Incirrina started in late 2017. Since both of us are professional musicians and music teachers, we’ve been involved in numerous bands and projects and music has always been the center of our lives, but neither of us had ever been in a purely synth band before. It was a great pleasure to discover already in our first meeting, in September 2014, that we had the exact same taste in music- we were talking for hours about Jean Michel Jarre, Joy Division, The Cure, Kraftwerk and numerous others… We became a couple, still the timing for forming a band wasn’t right yet- we were working hard in teaching and the other projects, and simply didn’t have the time to start something new together. But in 2017 life brought things together in such a way that conditions were created for something new to be born. Incirrina came into life with the aim to make music in the style we’ve deeply loved since we were teenagers. Irini: The first tracks were written right in our living room. Although I do write lyrics, we chose to base our songs on the poetry of William Blake, an artist we both deeply adore. After recording 6 songs, and without thinking twice, we uploaded them on Bandcamp (this was the first EP “8.15”; in December 2018), and suddenly something clicked. We received an unexpected wave of enthusiasm from complete strangers. Essentially, we started with no expectations other than making songs that we liked. It was magical how this evolved. One year later, in late 2019, the Greek label Geheimnis Records released “8.15” as an LP -the first 6 songs plus 5 new ones. Then COVID hit. During those strange years of isolation, we wrote the songs for our second album, “Lip Led Scream”, which was released by Cold Transmission in August 2022. One thing naturally led to another; some months before the lockdown, we had received an invitation to perform in Germany, in Slow Club Freiburg, a show that finally came to life in May 2022. That was the spark that started this beautiful adventure of European tours and live shows. In the years leading up to this year’s release of “Trace”, we focused on live performances as well as exploring new sounds and we also scored two theatrical plays in Athens. We are quite strict with our music , even though we compose new tracks very quickly, the ones we choose to release are very few (for every track we release, about four or five others are left behind). George: We really enjoy jamming and playing together, most of our tracks come alive through this very process. But there are also songs written entirely by one of us, then the other one enriched or reshaped them, regarding arrangement or structure. While we co-write the harmonic and melodic elements of our songs and handle the arrangements together, our individual roles are quite distinct. I focus on the rhythmic side, taking care of the live drums and drum programming, also the basslines and the riffs, while Irini handles the vocals. Q: One of the defining characteristics of your music is your use of analogue synthesizers. That seems like a very deliberate choice. What is it about analogue synths that continues to inspire you, and how has this aspect of your sound evolved over the years, particularly on “Trace”? George: Indeed, we have a great love for analog sound and analog synthesizers. Of course, there are plenty digital instruments we really like and also use. I adore Moog synthesizers, their rich harmonic sound fills the ear with very distinct frequencies. I love that you can never have the exact same sound. The instruments that I use do not have a ‘preset’ or ‘save’ possibility, so every time I make the sound from the beginning and I find this really thrilling. Analog synthesizers have personality; I feel like I’m using a sonic canvas when playing them, their sound has so many shades and details. Irini: We’ve used analog synths on all of our albums. In “Trace”, we paired them with acoustic instruments and also some digital synths, like the AKAI MPC and the Yamaha PS-55. Even though the Yamaha is digital, it’s from way back in 1983, and its sound has this nostalgic warmth that really speaks to us. Our relationship with instruments is just like with people… we have great chemistry and love for some, while others we just can’t connect with at all! An instrument is a whole world of its own, and a single sound can inspire an entire song. Some tracks started out just from a single sound, like the song “She Is In The Dream”. We also love building lots of layers and textures when it comes to orchestration, and our analog synths are perfect for mixing and layering in different ways. Q: Are you essentially a duo or more of a trio? I ask because I noticed that your lyrics are not always written by the two of you. Could you explain how that collaboration works, and how the lyrical themes develop in relation to your own musical ideas? Irini : Musically speaking, we’re definitely a duo; the two of us write and play all the music, and we handle everything that goes into running a band. But at the same time we also have a ‘secret’ third member. This is the poet Konstantinos Londos, whom we are lucky enough to have in our lives as a very special and dearly loved friend. He wrote the lyrics for our last two albums (with the exception of two songs, one on each record). Konstantinos puts what we feel and want to communicate into words in the most wonderful way. Working with him is magical. A lot of times we’ll discuss a topic that’s really on our minds, and then Konstantinos will write a poem about it… and just like that, we have the lyrics for a song. Other times, we picked some of his existing poems that spoke to our hearts, set them to music, and turned them into songs (like “Mutate” and “Alien Room”). But either way, there’s always an incredible creative process between the 3 of us – we listen together to the musical ideas, discuss the meaning of the lyrics, how the words flow melodically, and their deeper impact. In the end, after plenty of changes and fine-tuning (and sometimes after a lot of tears) the song finally takes its true shape. Konstantinos has a rare gift for clarity, simplicity, humor, sensitivity and working together with him is really a pleasure. He is an explosive mix of a brilliant Renaissance man, a Homo Universalis, and someone who genuinely prefers to stay out of the spotlight. Q: Speaking of the lyrics, “Trace” is an intriguing title that can be interpreted in many different ways. The album also explores profound and, at times, rather introspective themes. Could you tell us more about the concept behind the album? And to what extent do the lyrics shape the atmosphere of the music—or is it sometimes the other way around? Irini: Finding the right album title is usually a tricky process, since it needs to capture a lot of different concepts in just a few words. But with “Trace”, things were easier – the title came about completely spontaneously from Konstantinos, right after a chat about what making this album meant to us. The word means ‘imprint’; and that’s exactly what this record is: the footprint of a collaboration between people trying to capture in sounds and words the things that spark their thoughts and haunt their nights. This is also stated in the album’s back cover: “Trace”; is the imprint of ‘searching for wondrous , meaningful diversions , novel transformations  and transitory acts of care and defiance’. Thematically the songs deal with the uniqueness of human experience and the struggle of not losing one’s inner freedom and individuality in dystopian times – the ‘seeming real’; where all that is imposed and inhumane presents itself as the inevitable truth (“Always Here”). Celebrating diversity and self-expression, but always connecting and creating with other people, is a way out (“Mutate”). And the album itself is the result of such a process; we consider ourselves, against the odds, as artisans and friends who make music, share it and reinvent ourselves. Other songs cover universal, age-old themes like love, loneliness, the fear of loss, pain of death (“Sometimes”, “Region”), also the relationship with oneself and the connection with the world outside (“Diver”, “Find”), themes like the dream element, the urban landscape, and mysterious, fairy-like figures are touched upon in the songs “Alexia”, “Presence”, “She Is In The Dream”; burning issues of our time like domestic violence (“Alien Room”); and how the ‘self’ connects with today’s world, showing endless introspection but a lack of empathy, human pain, and the way we try to hide it even from ourselves (“ΚΡΥΦΟ”; – means “Hidden”); which is the only track in Greek language). George: Since songwriting is a two-way street, as we described earlier, the atmosphere that is created depends on each individual song. When we start composing music for an existing poem, we are influenced by the content, the meaning of the lyrics, and the rhythm of the words and syllables. Conversely, Konstantinos would often listen to a musical theme we had composed and write lyrics over it, based on a topic that was on our minds and that we had been discussing. However, since the general vibe of our music and lyrics is already introspective and relatively dark, we take it for granted that we won’t stray from that… not out of principle, but because the darker element simply speaks to us emotionally and temperamentally. Q: How do you approach your live performances? More specifically, how do you translate the layered studio recordings, and especially the analogue elements, to the stage? George: Βeing a duo has a lot of advantages, like flexibility with rehearsals, the creative process, and traveling. But also has plenty of challenges… Practically speaking, if we wanted to perform our tracks live with their full studio orchestration, we would definitely need at least one more musician on stage. Our compromise is to use backing tracks for the drums, or a portion of them while I play the rest, and then we perform the melodic and bass lines live. We inevitably have to skip several elements from the album… still that’s not necessarily a bad thing for a live performance, because different things take priority on stage. Also, for gigs, we bring along smaller gear. It would be practically impossible for just two people to travel carrying the actual instruments we used to compose and record, so we adapt our sound to smaller, more flexible instruments, which are a mix of analog, hybrid, and digital instruments. When we play in our hometown, things are much  easier and we can bring along some of the original (and heavy) instruments used in the recording. But when it comes to touring abroad, since we travel by plane and train, doing that would totally be out of the question for practical reasons. Irini: Over time, we’ve rearranged some tracks for our live shows to such an extent that they end up sounding quite different from the studio recordings, in terms of orchestration, tempo, and also vocals. This is especially true for songs from our first album. Also, since we love improvisation, we play the tracks a bit differently at almost every gig. We add intros, change up some riffs, and basically transform them depending on the mood of the moment. It would be really interesting at some point to make an album with our older songs exactly as they are played live, in a live recording setup. This happened already with one song , the “Only One Smile Alone”; the original one is “The Smile”; and following the suggestion of Andreas Hermann, we recorded it again in the way we play it live. Q: Finally, with an album title like “Trace”, it seems only natural to ask: what kind of trace do you hope this album—and Incirrina’s music in general—will leave behind? And what lies ahead for the band in the coming months? Ιrini: What we truly want with all our hearts is this: for people who will listen to our music, to feel something, to be moved, to dance, to feel good, or to find a personal meaning in our songs. Through our music, we aren’t seeking self-expression as much as we are seeking connection and co-motion, sharing in something as beautiful as music. We would love for the music of Incirrina to leave a small imprint of beauty in this world. Everything is fleeting and surely everything fades into the oblivion of time, but we would be incredibly happy if, even for just a few moments, we could bring joy to some people… just as we experience the joy of making songs and playing together, in rehearsals or in live shows. George: In the coming months, we will mainly focus on presenting “Trace” through live performances in Greece and Europe. We definitely want to work on producing some new songs as well, and we also plan to celebrate our 10th anniversary as a band with something special, which we will announce in early 2027…! Thank you for this interview, and we wish all the very best to you and your readers! Incirrina

items._cn_summary: 希腊二人组合Incirrina由George Katsanos和Irini Tiniakou于2017年在雅典成立，2026年通过德国独立厂牌Cold Transmission Music发行了第三张全长专辑《Trace》。他们的声音从早期的Dark-Wave逐渐演变，融合了Minimal-Synth和Post-Punk根基，发展出带有八十年代冷峻模拟质感的Minimal/Electro-Wave风格。Irini冰冷的嗓音是核心特征。专辑包含11首歌曲，使用模拟合成器、鼓机、电贝斯、电钢琴以及kantele、waterphone、melodica等原声乐器录制于24通道调音台，探索了乐器配置、节奏与人声表达的新路径，新作品在动态、深度和节奏多样性上有所拓展。这是两人作为职业音乐人和教师长期合作的延续，乐队被视为探索、实验和自我表达的空间。

items.body: Brian Stillman is an American artist based in New York who is releasing his debut album, “Terminal Days”, featuring nine tracks. The album is politically engaged, with a raised middle finger directed at fascists, oligarchs, tech bros, A.I. fetishists, and human rights abusers. The music sounds like pure, good old-fashioned Industrial-Metal. The guitar riffs leave no doubt about it, backed by hellish rhythms and vocals loaded with rage. Despite the sheer power of this Industrial-Metal assault, there are also a few more refined Pop arrangements to be found. This makes the whole thing highly accessible, but believe me, the album remains packed with adrenaline from start to finish. There is a fine balance between the guitar work and the synths, creating a powerful and dynamic sound. Ministry fans will undoubtedly appreciate this project. “Terminal Days” sounds like a very promising debut album, and Negative Agent is undoubtedly a name to keep in mind. (Rating:7)-. Listen to “Annihilation Kick”: https://negativeagent.bandcamp.com/track/annihilation-kick
items._cn_summary: Brian Stillman以Negative Agent之名发布首张专辑《Terminal Days》，收录九首作品。整张专辑带有强烈的政治批判色彩，矛头指向法西斯寡头、科技巨头及人权侵犯者，以金属化的工业之声宣泄愤怒。吉他riff猛烈、鼓击如地狱，配以充满怒意的唱腔，在合成器与吉他之间取得平衡，形成既有冲击力又不失流行可听性的动态声响。Ministry式的工业金属底色贯穿始终，但其中穿插更为精致的流行段落编排，使专辑在保持肾上腺素的同时拓宽了受众层面。作为首作，《Terminal Days》展示了作者在重型工业金属框架内融合流行旋律与电子合成器的能力，整体完成度高，能量充沛，是值得关注的新声音。

items.body:
More slick sophisti-pop from the CPH scene via GB aka Gustav Berntsen, kinda heavily reminds us of a Japanoise/ jazz fusion take on Sam Prekop’s self-titled alltimer with bits of Red House Painters, Steely Dan and Prefab Sprout in there too.

Berntsen was stationed in London when he was writing 'Herzprung' and began to collect copies of the infamous free rag Metro, that he cut to shreds to fix up the lyrical portion of the songs. Once he had this in check, the Danish singer-songwriter called up his most trusted collaborators and booked a week at a studio "in the Swedish wilderness", where he dubbed the songs live to 24-track tape, encouraging improvisation and collaboration. And there's certainly a knottiness to this material that's unique to Bernsten; like many contemporary Copenhagen-based operatives, he's clearly well versed in classic rock and pop, from Fleetwood Mac and Steely Dan to Chick Corea and Haruomi Hosono, but he doesn't stop at pastiche, instead bringing his own absurdities to the table. "The Simpson's Season Six," he calls out harmoniously on opener 'Adrenaline', interrupting a stop-start drum fill and riffs that wouldn't sound out of place on a Gastr del Sol record. 

It would be hard to label 'Herzprung' post-rock, but there's a sense that Berntsen has at least learned from the genre's Chicago-era excesses. He seems to be driven by a holistic understanding of pop; at their heart, his songs are impeccably written, yet he's also not interested in taking the clearest path. On 'Belly', his cool-headed harmonies and almost tropicalia-strength choruses are complicated by winding instrumental sections and a phenomenally atmospheric dip into tape-fuckt cosmic ambience, while the lengthy 'Shit River' is a slowcore anthem that Berntsen expands with a full choir and an arsenal of synths.
items._genre: sophisti-pop / jazz fusion / experimental pop / slowcore
items._cn_summary: 哥本哈根唱作人Gustav Berntsen的第二张专辑在伦敦和瑞典野外录音室完成，采用24轨磁带实时录制并鼓励即兴合作。他将伦敦免费报纸Metro剪碎拼贴作为歌词文本，这种解构文本的方式赋予作品独特的怪异性。音乐层面，Berntsen展现出对经典摇滚与流行的深厚功底，从Steely Dan到Chick Corea、Haruomi Hosono均有涉猎，但他拒绝单纯的风格模仿，转而注入个人化的荒诞感。开场曲'Adrenaline'中突然出现的'Simpson's Season Six'和声打断了Gastr del Sol式的riff段落；'Belly'以冷静和声和近似热带质感的副歌开头，随后滑入磁带实验性的宇宙氛围；长达数分钟的'Shit River'则是一首慢核颂歌，扩展为完整合唱团与合成器群的大编制编制。整体而言，这是一张融合了精致流行、爵士元素与实验意识的跨界作品。

items.body:
Barnt’s mnml 2012 kosmische waltzer for Matias Aguayo’s Cómeme is repackaged with a new master and Jens-Uwe Beyer + Crato revisions.

The kinky schaeffel is in effect on ‘gaffe’, which takes on a 2nd wind in its brighter, robust remaster, while Jens Uwe-Beyer evens out its irregularities for a disco-ready remix, and best of all, a ‘Magazine Hallucination’ mix that initially jettisons the beat and opens upwards, outward into majestic ambient zones, before its pulled back in a screwed echo of the original waltz groove.
items._cn_summary: Barnt 2012年发行的迷你这张作品由 Matias Aguayo 的 Cómeme 厂牌再版发行，附带全新母带处理以及 Jens-Uwe Beyer 与 Crato 的混音修订。'gaffe' 这首作品在新版母带中呈现出更明亮、饱满的听感，Jens-Uwe Beyer 将其原有的不规则起伏打磨为适合舞池的流畅版本。最为突出的是 'Magazine Hallucination' 混音，初始剥离节奏结构，向开阔的 ambient 氛围延展，随后再以扭曲回声的形式将原作的圆舞曲律动拉回主轴。整体在极简电子与宇宙感氛围之间切换，展现出结构拆解与重组的创作思路，对迷你和电子融合方向具备一定吸引力。

items.body:
Cranky UKG bassbin permutations by a producer with form for Keysound, making his mark on Bristol-via-Berlin’s Sneaker Social Club.

Bare bones rhythms clack and swang in ‘Vintage Gilly’, where aspects of post-dubstep minimalism, electrified halfstep, dark garage and gqom tesselate with a rude UK torque. He recalls Basic Rhythms asceticism on the angular, staccato grime hunch of ‘Drift into Dread’, and the title tune’s rictus, concentrated halfstep, rubbed with Zomby-esque melody, wheres ‘Godkiller’ gives it up for El-B and Sully style darker garage swivel, and ‘Glass Eater’ trades in a sort of warped UKG x gqom mutation.

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑呈现了英式车库舞曲与低音音乐的解构重组，融合了后dubstep极简主义、电子化半步舞曲、暗潮车库以及南非gqom的碎片化节奏语汇。制作人曾在Keysound厂牌发表作品，风格上呼应Basic Rhythm的苦行式节奏美学和Zomby式的旋律碎片处理。专辑中各曲目侧重点不同：标题曲以紧绷的半步节拍配合尖锐旋律线条，'Godkiller'回归El-B与Sully式的暗色车库旋转律动，'Glass Eater'则尝试UKG与gqom的变异融合。整体制作偏向骨骼式的节奏骨架，剔除多余修饰，以棱角分明的断奏节奏和低频扭矩为核心驱动。Sneaker Social Club作为Bristol与柏林跨地的独立小厂牌，为这类地下低音实验提供了恰当的发行渠道。
